characters.description: Father of Creon and Jocasta.

characters.name: Epicasta
characters.description: Homer's name for Jocasta; married her son Oedipus; hanged herself.

characters.name: Nycteis
characters.description: Wife of Polydorus; mentioned in the genealogy.

characters.name: Athamas
characters.description: Husband of Ino; mentioned in the genealogy.

characters.name: Learchus
characters.description: Son of Ino and Athamas; mentioned in the genealogy.

characters.name: Melicertes
characters.description: Son of Ino and Athamas; mentioned in the genealogy.

characters.name: Menoeceus I
characters.description: Father of Creon and Jocasta; mentioned in the genealogy.

characters.name: Menoeceus II
characters.description: Son of Creon; mentioned in the genealogy.

characters.name: Haemon
characters.description: Son of Creon; mentioned in the genealogy.

characters.name: Capaneus
characters.description: One of the Seven against Thebes; boasted he would burn the city, killed by Zeus' thunderbolt.
major_myths: Theseus as Champion of the Oppressed

characters.name: Hippomedon
characters.description: One of the Seven against Thebes.

characters.name: Hypsipyle
characters.description: Nurse of Opheltes; led the Seven to a spring; former queen of Lemnos, mother of Thoas and Euneos by Jason.

characters.name: Opheltes
characters.description: Infant son of King Lycurgus of Nemea; killed by a serpent while Hypsipyle guided the Seven.

characters.name: Thoas
characters.description: Son of Hypsipyle and Jason; arrived at Nemea and took Hypsipyle back to Lemnos.

characters.name: Euneos
characters.description: Son of Hypsipyle and Jason; arrived at Nemea and took Hypsipyle back to Lemnos.

characters.name: Aethra
characters.description: Mother of Theseus; helped persuade Theseus to aid the suppliants.
major_myths: Theseus as Champion of the Oppressed

characters.name: Justice
characters.description: Personified justice; Antigone invokes her as the source of divine law.

characters.name: Argia
characters.description: Widow of Polynices; in Euripides' version, helps Antigone bury Polynices.

characters.name: Maeon
characters.description: Son of Antigone and Haemon in Euripides' version.

characters.name: Alcmaeon
characters.description: Son of Amphiaraüs and Eriphyle; led the Epigoni and killed his mother; later killed by sons of Phegeus.

characters.name: Eueres
characters.description: Theban nobleman; father of Tiresias.

characters.name: Amphitryon
characters.description: Husband of Alcmene; summoned Tiresias to interpret the infant Heracles strangling snakes.

characters.name: Phegeus
characters.description: King of Arcadia; father of Alcmaeon's first wife; his sons killed Alcmaeon.

characters.name: Myrtilus
characters.description: Son of Hermes, charioteer of Oenomaüs; helped Pelops by sabotaging Oenomaüs' chariot; attempted to violate Hippodamia and was killed by Pelops; cursed Pelops and his descendants.
major_myths: The Race of Pelops and Oenomaüs

characters.name: Aërope
characters.description: Wife of Atreus; committed adultery with Thyestes and gave him the golden-fleeced ram.
major_myths: The Quarrel of Atreus and Thyestes

characters.name: Chrysothemis
characters.description: Daughter of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra; important only as a foil for Electra in Sophocles' play.

characters.name: Pelopia
characters.description: Daughter of Thyestes; mother of Aegisthus by her father Thyestes.

characters.name: Amphithea
characters.description: Queen of Sicyon; comforts Pelopia in a vase painting.

characters.name: Leda
characters.description: Mother of Helen and the Dioscuri; married to Tyndareus.
major_myths: Birth of the Dioscuri and Helen

characters.name: Tyndareus
characters.description: Husband of Leda; father of Helen and the Dioscuri.
major_myths: Birth of the Dioscuri and Helen

characters.name: Dioscuri
characters.description: Sons of Leda and Tyndareus (or Zeus); brothers of Helen.

characters.name: Hermione
characters.description: Daughter of Helen and Menelaüs; married to Neoptolemus then Orestes.

characters.name: Strophius
characters.description: King of Phocis, with whom Orestes grew up in exile.

characters.name: Polydeuces
characters.description: Brother of Helen, immortalized with Castor.
major_myths: Quarrel of the Dioscuri with Idas and Lynceus

characters.name: Cilissa
characters.description: Nurse of Orestes.

characters.name: Tisamenus
characters.description: Son of Orestes and Hermione, led Achaeans against Heraclidae.

characters.name: Menelaus
characters.description: Husband of Helen, brother of Agamemnon.

characters.name: Eris
characters.description: Goddess of Discord; threw the golden apple inscribed 'For the most beautiful' at the wedding of Peleus and Thetis.

characters.name: Lynceus
characters.description: Son of Aphareus; quarreled with the Dioscuri; killed Castor.
major_myths: Quarrel of the Dioscuri with Idas and Lynceus

characters.name: Stesichorus
characters.description: Seventh-century poet; invented the version that Helen went to Egypt, not Troy.

characters.name: Aphareus
characters.description: Father of Idas and Lynceus.
major_myths: Quarrel of the Dioscuri with Idas and Lynceus

characters.name: Himeros
characters.description: Personification of desire; child of Aphrodite.

characters.name: Laomedon
characters.description: King of Troy; cheated Apollo and Poseidon of their pay; killed by Heracles.

characters.name: Hesione
characters.description: Daughter of Laomedon; saved by Heracles from sea monster; given to Telamon as wife.

characters.name: Telamon
characters.description: Greek hero; companion of Heracles; married Hesione; father of Teucer and Ajax.

characters.name: Podarces
characters.description: Young son of Laomedon; spared by Heracles; later became king Priam.
major_myths: Melampus and the Cattle of Phylacus

characters.name: Oenone
characters.description: Nymph with healing powers; first love of Paris; refused to heal him and killed herself.

characters.name: Philoctetes
characters.description: Greek hero; wounded Paris with an arrow.

characters.name: Astyanax
characters.description: Son of Hector and Andromache; killed in the fall of Troy.

characters.name: Eëtion
characters.description: Ally of Troy; father of Andromache; killed by Achilles.

characters.name: Troïlus
characters.description: Son of Priam; killed by Achilles.

characters.name: Polyxena
characters.description: Daughter of Priam; sacrificed on the tomb of Achilles after the sack of Troy.

characters.name: Antenor
characters.description: Brother of Hecuba; advised returning Helen; spared by Greeks; founded Patavium.

characters.name: Theano
characters.description: Wife of Antenor; priestess of Athena.

characters.name: Sarpedon
characters.description: Son of Zeus and Laodamia; Lycian leader; killed by Patroclus; body saved by Zeus.

characters.name: Sleep
characters.description: Personification of sleep; twin of Death; carried Sarpedon's body.

characters.name: Death
characters.description: Personification of death; twin of Sleep; carried Sarpedon's body.

characters.name: Rhesus
characters.description: Son of one of the Muses, Thracian leader, killed by Diomedes and Odysseus.

characters.name: Dolon
characters.description: Trojan spy, caught and killed by Diomedes and Odysseus.

characters.name: Ajax the Greater
characters.description: Son of Telamon, second only to Achilles as a warrior.

characters.name: Ajax the Less
characters.description: Son of Oïleus, prince of the Locrians, violated Cassandra.

characters.name: Idomeneus
characters.description: Son of Deucalion, leader of the Cretans, voluntary ally of Agamemnon.

characters.name: Palamedes
characters.description: Greek envoy who uncovered Odysseus' feigned madness.

characters.name: Memnon
characters.description: Ethiopian leader, killed Antilochus.

characters.name: Antilochus
characters.description: Son of Nestor, killed by Memnon.

characters.name: Meriones
characters.description: Greek warrior, helped Menelaüs retreat with Patroclus' body.

characters.name: Oïleus
characters.description: Father of Ajax the Less.

characters.name: Hypnos
characters.description: God of sleep, depicted carrying Sarpedon's body.

characters.name: Phocus
characters.description: Half-brother of Peleus, killed by Peleus.

characters.name: Eurytion
characters.description: King of Phthia who purified Peleus and gave him part of his kingdom; accidentally killed by Peleus during the Calydonian boar hunt.

characters.name: Acastus
characters.description: Son of Pelias, king of Iolcus; purified Peleus after the death of Eurytion.

characters.name: Astydamia
characters.description: Wife of Acastus; fell in love with Peleus and falsely accused him of seduction.

characters.name: Deïdamia
characters.description: Daughter of Lycomedes, mother of Neoptolemus by Achilles.

characters.name: Lycomedes
characters.description: King of Scyros, father of Deïdamia; Achilles was disguised among his daughters.

characters.name: Phoenix
characters.description: Tutor and companion of Achilles; fled to Peleus after being cursed by his father.

characters.name: Poeas
characters.description: Father of Philoctetes; lit the funeral pyre of Heracles and received his bow and arrows.

characters.name: Podalirius
characters.description: Son of Asclepius; healed Philoctetes' wound.

characters.name: Agyrtes
characters.description: Trumpeter who sounded the alarm at Scyros to reveal Achilles.

characters.name: Protesilaüs
characters.description: First Greek to leap ashore at Troy, killed by Hector.
major_myths: Melampus and the Cattle of Phylacus

characters.name: Euphorbus
characters.description: Trojan who wounds Patroclus with a spear.

characters.name: Meleager
characters.description: Hero from Calydon; parallel to Achilles in Phoenix's speech.

characters.name: Mynes
characters.description: First husband of Briseïs, killed by Achilles.

characters.name: Automedon
characters.description: Charioteer of Achilles.

characters.name: Xanthus
characters.description: Achilles' horse, who prophesies his death.

characters.name: Penthesilea
characters.description: Queen of the Amazons, led a contingent to help Troy, killed by Achilles.

characters.name: Sinon
characters.description: Greek left behind to deceive Trojans about the horse.

characters.name: Laocoön
characters.description: Son of Antenor and priest of Apollo; hurled spear into horse and was killed by serpents.

characters.name: Ascanius
characters.description: Son of Aeneas who escaped Troy.

characters.name: Ajax the Locrian
characters.description: Son of Oïleus, dragged Cassandra from temple of Athena; killed by gods on way home.

characters.name: Polymestor
characters.description: Thracian king who murdered Polydorus and was blinded by Hecuba.

characters.name: Creusa
characters.description: Wife of Aeneas, lost during the escape from Troy; her ghost appeared to Aeneas.

characters.name: Tritonian Pallas
characters.description: Athena, took up her place on Troy's citadel, lit with storm-cloud and Gorgon.

characters.name: Father of the gods
characters.description: Zeus, renewed the courage of the Greeks and urged them to fight.

characters.name: Althaea
characters.description: Mother of Meleager, prayed for his death and burned the log that determined his life.

characters.name: Oeneus
characters.description: King of Calydon, father of Meleager and Deïanira, offended Artemis.

characters.name: Schoeneus
characters.description: Boeotian king, father of Atalanta.

characters.name: Cleopatra
characters.description: Wife of Meleager, begged him to return to battle, hanged herself after his death.

characters.name: Deïanira
characters.description: Sister of Meleager, wife of Heracles.

characters.name: Iphiclus
characters.description: Brother of Althaea, killed by Meleager in battle.
major_myths: Melampus and the Cattle of Phylacus

characters.name: Aphares
characters.description: Brother of Althaea, killed by Meleager in battle.

characters.name: Milanion
characters.description: Companion of Atalanta on the François Vase, who wins her as his bride in another tale.

characters.name: Troilus
characters.description: Trojan prince, pursued by Achilles on the François Vase.

characters.name: Polites
characters.description: Trojan warrior, emerges from Troy on the François Vase.

characters.name: Damasippus
characters.description: Participant in the chariot race on the François Vase.

characters.name: Nauplius
characters.description: Avenged death of his son Palamedes by luring ships onto rocks with false beacon.

characters.name: Aegialia
characters.description: Daughter of Adrastus; wife of Diomedes; unfaithful due to Aphrodite's anger.

characters.name: Daunus
characters.description: Apulian king who gave land to Diomedes in Italy.

characters.name: Latinus
characters.description: King whom Diomedes declined to help against Aeneas.

characters.name: Meda
characters.description: Wife of Idomeneus; committed adultery with Leucus.

characters.name: Leucus
characters.description: Adulterer with Meda; murdered her and her daughter; made himself king of ten Cretan cities.

characters.name: Maron
characters.description: Priest of Apollo at Ismarus; spared by Odysseus; gave him twelve jars of wine.

characters.name: Laestrygonians
characters.description: Giant cannibals encountered by Odysseus.

characters.name: Telegonus
characters.description: Son of Odysseus and Circe.

characters.name: Gorgon
characters.description: Monster whose head turns all who behold it to stone; Odysseus feared its appearance in the Underworld.

characters.name: Leucothea
characters.description: Sea-goddess, formerly the mortal Ino, daughter of Cadmus; helped Odysseus reach Scheria.

characters.name: Nausicaä
characters.description: Daughter of Alcinoüs; found Odysseus on the shore and brought him to the palace.

characters.name: Arete
characters.description: Queen of the Phaeacians, wife of Alcinoüs.

characters.name: Laertes
characters.description: Father of Odysseus; Penelope wove a burial garment for him.

characters.name: Eumaeus
characters.description: Odysseus' faithful swineherd who gave him refuge.

characters.name: Irus
characters.description: Beggar who insulted Odysseus and was knocked out in a fight.

characters.name: Euryclea
characters.description: Odysseus' old nurse who recognized him by his scar.
major_myths: The Bow and the Killing of the Suitors

characters.name: Antinoüs
characters.description: Leader of the suitors, killed by Odysseus.
major_myths: The Bow and the Killing of the Suitors

characters.name: Medon
characters.description: Herald spared by Odysseus after the killing of the suitors.
major_myths: The Bow and the Killing of the Suitors

characters.name: Melanthius
characters.description: Disloyal goatherd mutilated and killed by Odysseus.
major_myths: The Bow and the Killing of the Suitors

characters.name: Mentes
characters.description: Disguise used by Athena when visiting Telemachus.

characters.name: Amphimedon
characters.description: One of the leading suitors of Penelope. His ghost tells Agamemnon of the slaughter.

characters.name: Eupeithes
characters.description: Father of Antinoüs. Killed by Laertes during the final battle.

characters.name: Cicones
characters.description: People attacked by Odysseus after leaving Troy.

characters.name: Lotus-eaters
characters.description: People who eat lotus fruit, causing forgetfulness. Odysseus visits their land.

characters.name: Phaeacians
characters.description: People who honor Odysseus and send him home to Ithaca with gifts.

characters.name: Macareus
characters.description: Son of Aeolus; fell in love with his sister Canace; committed suicide.

characters.name: Canace
characters.description: Daughter of Aeolus; mother of Macareus's child; killed herself with a sword.

characters.name: Phoroneus
characters.description: First of men, established the kingdom of Argos, decided in favor of Hera in the contest between Poseidon and Hera.

characters.name: Hypermnestra
characters.description: Daughter of Danaüs, alone did not kill her husband.

characters.name: Danaë
characters.description: Daughter of Acrisius, mother of Perseus by Zeus.
major_myths: Polydectes and Perseus' Return to Argos

characters.name: Acrisius
characters.description: King of Argos, father of Danaë, killed by his grandson Perseus.

characters.name: Abas
characters.description: Great-grandfather of Perseus, father of twin sons Proetus and Acrisius.

characters.name: Dictys
characters.description: Fisherman of Seriphos who rescued Danaë and Perseus.
major_myths: Polydectes and Perseus' Return to Argos

characters.name: Polydectes
characters.description: King of Seriphos, brother of Dictys, fell in love with Danaë, sent Perseus to fetch Gorgon's head.
major_myths: Polydectes and Perseus' Return to Argos

characters.name: Andromeda
characters.description: Daughter of Cepheus and Cassiepea, rescued by Perseus from sea-monster.

characters.name: Cepheus
characters.description: King of Ethiopia or Levant, father of Andromeda.

characters.name: Cassiepea
characters.description: Queen, mother of Andromeda, boasted she was more beautiful than the Nereids.

characters.name: Belus
characters.description: Son of Epaphus and Libya, father of Aegyptus and Danaüs.

characters.name: Apis
characters.description: Son of Niobe and Zeus.

characters.name: Aegyptus
characters.description: Son of Belus, father of fifty sons.

characters.name: Libya
characters.description: Daughter of Epaphus, mother of Belus and Agenor.

characters.name: Cassiopeia
characters.description: Queen of Ethiopia, mother of Andromeda, boasted of her beauty.

characters.name: Phineus
characters.description: Brother of Cepheus, previously betrothed to Andromeda, opposed Perseus and was turned to stone.

characters.name: Megapenthes
characters.description: Son of Proetus, exchanged kingdoms with Perseus.

characters.name: Eurystheus
characters.description: Descendant of Perseus, king of Mycenae, set labors for Heracles.

characters.name: Amymone
characters.description: A Danaïd sent by her father to search for water; saved by Poseidon who lay with her and caused a spring to burst from a rock.

characters.name: Stheneboea
characters.description: Wife of Proetus (called Antea by Homer); fell in love with Bellerophon and falsely accused him; later killed by Bellerophon.

characters.name: Iobates
characters.description: King of Lycia, father-in-law of Proetus; received sealed letter and sent Bellerophon on dangerous missions.

characters.name: Chimera
characters.description: Monster with lion's forepart, serpent's tail, and goat's middle; breathed fire; killed by Bellerophon.

characters.name: Solymi
characters.description: A people fought by Bellerophon.

characters.name: Amazons
characters.description: Legendary race of warrior women; fought and slain by Bellerophon.

characters.name: Hippolochus
characters.description: Son of Bellerophon, father of Glaucus.

characters.name: Isandrus
characters.description: Son of Bellerophon, killed fighting the Solymi.

characters.name: Eumelos
characters.description: Corinthian poet who identified Homer's Ephyra with Corinth.

characters.name: Aeëtes
characters.description: Son of Helius, founder of Corinth according to Eumelos.

characters.name: Iphicles
characters.description: Mortal twin brother of Heracles, son of Amphitryon and Alcmena.

characters.name: Iolaüs
characters.description: Nephew of Heracles, son of Iphicles, helped Heracles in the Lernaean Hydra labor.

characters.name: Linus
characters.description: Son of Apollo, music teacher of Heracles, killed by Heracles with a lyre.

characters.name: Thespius
characters.description: King of Thespiae, entertained Heracles during the lion hunt; Heracles lay with his fifty daughters.

characters.name: Eurytus
characters.description: Taught Heracles archery.

characters.name: Cerynean Hind
characters.description: Golden-horned hind sacred to Artemis, captured by Heracles after a year-long pursuit.

characters.name: Erymanthian Boar
characters.description: Destructive boar from Mt. Erymanthus, captured alive by Heracles.

characters.name: Phyleus
characters.description: Son of Augeas, took Heracles' side in the quarrel, later made king of Elis by Heracles.

characters.name: Pholus
characters.description: Centaur who entertained Heracles; accidentally killed by a poisoned arrow.

characters.name: Dexamenus
characters.description: Nearby prince who received Heracles after the Augean stables labor; Heracles saved his daughter from the centaur Eurytion.

characters.name: Taÿgete
characters.description: Daughter of Atlas, who stamped Artemis' name on the golden horns of the Cerynean Hind.

characters.name: Electryon
characters.description: King of Mycenae, father of Alcmena, accidentally killed by Amphitryon.

characters.name: Pterelaüs
characters.description: King of the Teleboans, killed by Amphitryon after his daughter Comaetho removed his golden hair.

characters.name: Comaetho
characters.description: Daughter of Pterelaüs, betrayed her father out of love for Amphitryon, then killed by him.

characters.name: Sthenelus
characters.description: King of Mycenae, grandson of Zeus, father of Eurystheus.

characters.name: Sosia
characters.description: Servant of Amphitryon in Plautus' play, impersonated by Mercury.

characters.name: Bromia
characters.description: Servant of Alcmena in Plautus' play, describes the serpent-strangling scene.

characters.name: Hippolyta
characters.description: Queen of the Amazons, killed by Heracles for her girdle.

characters.name: Cacus
characters.description: Italian fire god who stole Geryon's cattle from Heracles.

characters.name: Eryx
characters.description: King of a mountain in Sicily, wrestled and killed by Heracles.

characters.name: Agathyrsus
characters.description: Son of Heracles and Echidna, driven away by Echidna.

characters.name: Gelonus
characters.description: Son of Heracles and Echidna, driven away by Echidna.

characters.name: Scythes
characters.description: Son of Heracles and Echidna, became king and ancestor of the Scythians.

characters.name: Pero
characters.description: Daughter of Neleus, bride-price was the cattle of Phylacus.
major_myths: Melampus and the Cattle of Phylacus

characters.name: Phylacus
characters.description: King of Phylace, owner of the cattle and father of Iphiclus.
major_myths: Melampus and the Cattle of Phylacus

characters.name: Omphale
characters.description: Queen of Lydia, Heracles served her as a slave.

characters.name: Busiris
characters.description: King of Egypt who sacrificed strangers to Zeus; killed by Heracles on his journey to the Hesperides.

characters.name: Syleus
characters.description: Robber who forced passers-by to work in his vineyard; killed by Heracles.

characters.name: Cercopes
characters.description: Pair of dwarfs who played tricks; caught by Heracles but released after making him laugh.

characters.name: Iphitus
characters.description: Brother of Iole; came to Tiryns searching for lost mares and was thrown from the citadel by Heracles.

characters.name: Periclymenus
characters.description: Son of Neleus; given the ability to transform by Poseidon; killed by Heracles when in the form of a bee.

characters.name: Hippocoön
characters.description: King of Sparta who assisted Neleus; attacked by Heracles.

characters.name: Auge
characters.description: Priestess of Athena; mother of Telephus by Heracles; set adrift in a chest with her son.

characters.name: Aegimius
characters.description: King of the Dorians; Heracles allied with him against the Lapiths and Dryopes.

characters.name: Nessus
characters.description: Centaur who attempted to violate Deianira; shot by Heracles; his blood later used by Deianira as a love charm.

characters.name: Hyllus
characters.description: Son of Heracles and Deianira.

characters.name: Macaria
characters.description: Daughter of Heracles and Deianira.

characters.name: Iole
characters.description: Daughter of Eurytus; Heracles fell in love with her; her father refused to give her to him.

characters.name: Ceyx
characters.description: King who received Heracles and Deïanira in Trachis.

characters.name: Lichas
characters.description: Herald who brought news of Oechalia and delivered the poisoned robe to Heracles.

characters.name: Lyssa
characters.description: Goddess sent by Hera to torment Heracles in Euripides' play.

characters.name: Prodicus of Ceos
characters.description: Philosopher who told the parable of Heracles' choice between Pleasure and Virtue.

characters.name: Virtue
characters.description: Personification of virtue in Prodicus' parable.

characters.name: Melkart
characters.description: Phoenician god identified with Heracles by Herodotus.

characters.name: Samson
characters.description: Israelite hero compared to Heracles.

characters.name: Sandas
characters.description: Cilician god compared to Heracles.

characters.name: Indra
characters.description: Indian hero who killed a three-headed monster, compared to Heracles.

characters.name: Visvarupa
characters.description: Three-headed monster killed by Indra.

characters.name: Demophon
characters.description: Son of Theseus, king of Athens who received Alcmena and her grandchildren according to Euripides.

characters.name: Echemus
characters.description: King of Tegea who killed Hyllus in single combat.

characters.name: Temenus
characters.description: Heraclid leader who consulted the oracle and led the successful invasion of the Peloponnese, received Argos, killed by his sons.

characters.name: Oxylus
characters.description: Aetolian exile who guided the Heraclids, found riding a one-eyed horse.

characters.name: Procles
characters.description: Son of Aristodemus, received Lacedaemon (Sparta), founder of one royal house.

characters.name: Eurysthenes
characters.description: Son of Aristodemus, received Lacedaemon (Sparta), founder of one royal house.

characters.name: Aristodemus
characters.description: Heraclid leader who died before the division of the conquered lands.

characters.name: Cresphontes
characters.description: Heraclid who received Messene, murdered by Polyphontes along with two of his sons.

characters.name: Polyphontes
characters.description: Rival Heraclid who murdered Cresphontes and forced Merope to marry him.

characters.name: Aepytus
characters.description: Surviving son of Cresphontes, raised in Aetolia, returned to kill Polyphontes and reclaim his father's throne.

characters.name: Augustus
characters.description: Roman emperor identified with Heracles by Horace.

characters.name: Nero
characters.description: Roman emperor who planned to fight a Nemean lion in the guise of Heracles.

characters.name: Commodus
characters.description: Roman emperor who portrayed himself as Heracles.

characters.name: Henri IV
characters.description: King of France welcomed into Avignon as the Gallic Heracles.

characters.name: Hesperus
characters.description: Personification of the evening star, associated with the Hesperides.

characters.name: Galanthis
characters.description: Servant of Alcmena who broke Eileithyia's spell, turned into a weasel.

characters.name: Erichthonius
characters.description: Early Attic king, partly serpent-shaped, sprung from the earth from Hephaestus' semen. Instituted Panathenaea and set up wooden statue of Athena.

characters.name: Pandrosos
characters.description: Daughter of Cecrops, one of the three sisters entrusted with Erichthonius.

characters.name: Auglauros
characters.description: Daughter of Cecrops, one of the three sisters. Later turned into a rock by Hermes for envy.

characters.name: Herse
characters.description: Daughter of Cecrops, loved by Hermes, mother of Cephalus.

characters.name: Philomela
characters.description: Daughter of Pandion, sister of Procne. Violated and silenced by Tereus, wove her story into a tapestry.

characters.name: Procne
characters.description: Daughter of Pandion, wife of Tereus, mother of Itys.

characters.name: Tereus
characters.description: Thracian king, husband of Procne, father of Itys. Violated Philomela and cut out her tongue.

characters.name: Itys
characters.description: Son of Tereus and Procne.

characters.name: Pandion
characters.description: Successor of Erichthonius, father of Philomela and Procne.

characters.name: Praxithea
characters.description: Wife of Erechtheus, approved sacrifice of their daughters.

characters.name: Laelaps
characters.description: Magic hound that always caught its quarry, given to Procris by Artemis.

characters.name: Orithyia
characters.description: Daughter of Erechtheus, loved by Boreas, carried off to Thrace; mother of Zetes, Calaïs, Cleopatra, Chione.

characters.name: Zetes
characters.description: Winged hero, son of Boreas and Orithyia; Argonaut.

characters.name: Calaïs
characters.description: Winged hero, son of Boreas and Orithyia; Argonaut.

characters.name: Chione
characters.description: Daughter of Boreas and Orithyia, mother of Eumolpus by Poseidon.

characters.name: Metion
characters.description: Uncle of Pandion (the later king); drove Pandion out of Attica.

characters.name: Periphetes
characters.description: Brigand, son of Hephaestus, armed with a club; killed by Theseus at Epidaurus.

characters.name: Cercyon
characters.description: Local hero at Eleusis; forced travelers to wrestle to the death; killed by Theseus.

characters.name: Procrustes
characters.description: Brigand between Eleusis and Athens; stretched or cut victims to fit his bed; killed by Theseus.

characters.name: Medus
characters.description: Son of Medea and Aegeus; rival to Theseus for succession.

characters.name: Polypemon
characters.description: Possibly father of Procrustes; mentioned in Bacchylides.

characters.name: Hecale
characters.description: Old woman who entertained Theseus on his way to Marathon; she promised to sacrifice to Zeus if Theseus returned successful, but died before his return.

characters.name: Androgeos
characters.description: Son of King Minos of Crete, killed in Attica due to jealousy over his victories at the Panathenaic games.

characters.name: Eriboea
characters.description: One of the Athenian maidens on the voyage to Crete, attacked by Minos.

characters.name: Menestheus
characters.description: Regent of Athens who instituted a cult in honor of the Dioscuri.

characters.name: Acamas
characters.description: Son of Theseus and Phaedra.

characters.name: Cimon
characters.description: Athenian leader; captured Scyros and brought Theseus' bones back to Athens.

characters.name: Phyllis
characters.description: Thracian princess; loved Demophon, hanged herself and became an almond tree.

characters.name: Codrus
characters.description: Last king of Athens; sacrificed himself for his city by provoking enemy soldiers to kill him.

characters.name: Daedalus
characters.description: Skilled craftsman and inventor, son or grandson of Metion; built the Labyrinth and wings for escape.

characters.name: Perdix
characters.description: Nephew of Daedalus; invented the saw, was thrown from a rock by Daedalus and turned into a partridge.

characters.name: Icarus
characters.description: Son of Daedalus; flew too close to the sun, his wax wings melted, and he fell into the sea.

characters.name: Cocalus
characters.description: King of the Sicilian city of Camicus, who received Daedalus.

characters.name: Catreus
characters.description: Son of Minos and Pasiphaë, became Cretan king, father of Althaemenes and Apemosyne.

characters.name: Althaemenes
characters.description: Son of Catreus, fled to Rhodes with his sister Apemosyne to avoid killing his father, but eventually killed Catreus accidentally. Honored as a hero by Rhodians.

characters.name: Apemosyne
characters.description: Daughter of Catreus, sister of Althaemenes, seduced by Hermes and killed by Althaemenes for apparent unchastity.

characters.name: Polyidus
characters.description: Seer who found Glaucus' corpse and restored him to life using an herb, then taught Glaucus the seer's art.

characters.name: Phrixus
characters.description: Son of Athamas and Nephele, rescued by the golden-fleeced ram, later married Chalciope in Colchis.

characters.name: Helle
characters.description: Daughter of Athamas and Nephele, fell off the golden ram into the straits later called Hellespont.

characters.name: Chalciope
characters.description: Elder daughter of Aeëtes, wife of Phrixus, mother of Argus, Melas, Phrontis, and Cytisorus.

characters.name: Melas
characters.description: Son of Phrixus and Chalciope.

characters.name: Phrontis
characters.description: Son of Phrixus and Chalciope.

characters.name: Cytisorus
characters.description: Son of Phrixus and Chalciope.

characters.name: Polymede
characters.description: Mother of Jason, wife of Aeson.

characters.name: Idmon
characters.description: Seer among the Argonauts, killed by a boar in the land of the Mariandyni.

characters.name: Euphemus
characters.description: Son of Poseidon, Argonaut who could run over waves without getting his feet wet.

characters.name: Tiphys
characters.description: Helmsman of the Argo, died during the voyage.

characters.name: Cyzicus
characters.description: King of the Doliones, received the Argonauts hospitably but was killed by them in a night battle.

characters.name: Amycus
characters.description: Son of Poseidon, king of the Bebryces, a boxer who forced strangers to fight him and was killed by Polydeuces.

characters.name: Ancaeus
characters.description: Arcadian hero, son of Lycurgus, became helmsman of the Argo after Tiphys died.

characters.name: Apsyrtus
characters.description: Brother of Medea, killed by Jason in an ambush near the mouth of the Danube.

characters.name: Aloeus
characters.description: Brother of Aeëtes, son of Helius and Antiope, inherited Arcadia.

characters.name: Talus
characters.description: Bronze giant who guarded Crete, walking around it three times a day and throwing rocks at strangers; his life depended on a membrane near his ankle.

characters.name: Arcesilas
characters.description: King of Cyrene, winner of the chariot race at Delphi in 462 B.C., to whom Pindar's poem is addressed.

characters.name: Glauce
characters.description: Daughter of Creon, second wife of Jason, killed by Medea's poisoned gifts.

characters.name: Hercules
characters.description: Participant in the Argonautic expedition, rescued Hesione with Telamon.

characters.name: Chorus
characters.description: Group of Corinthian women who comment on the action.

characters.name: Messenger
characters.description: Reports the deaths of Creusa and Creon to Medea.

characters.name: Aurora
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Eos.

characters.name: Helena
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Helen.

characters.name: Ceres
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Demeter.

characters.name: Hekabe
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Hecuba.

characters.name: Ulysses
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Odysseus.

characters.name: Minerva
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Athena.

characters.name: Mars
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Ares.

characters.name: Nyx
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Night.

characters.name: Hemera
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Day.

characters.name: Musae
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Muses.

characters.name: Ops
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Rhea.

characters.name: Justitia
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Themis.

characters.name: Moneta
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Mnemosyne.

characters.name: Sol
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Helius.

characters.name: Luna
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Selene.

characters.name: Latona
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Leto.

characters.name: Magna Mater
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Cybele.

characters.name: Terra
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Ge.

characters.name: Vesta
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Hestia.

characters.name: Trivia
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Hecate.

characters.name: Rhamnusia
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Nemesis.

characters.name: Victoria
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Nike.

characters.name: Gratiae
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Graces.

characters.name: Suada
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Persuasion.

characters.name: Parcae
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Fates.

characters.name: Grace
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Charis.

characters.name: Orthrus
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Orthus.

characters.name: Voluptas
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Pleasure.

characters.name: Concordia
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Harmonia.

characters.name: Bacchae
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Maenads.

characters.name: Pyrrhus
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Neoptolemus.

characters.name: Deiphobus
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Deïphobus.

characters.name: Hymenaeus
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Hymen.

characters.name: Dea Syria
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Atargatis.

characters.name: Castor and Pollux
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Dioscuri.

characters.name: Discordia
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Eris.

characters.name: Desire
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Himeros.

characters.name: Somnus
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Sleep.

characters.name: Deianira
characters.description: Roman equivalent of Deïanira.

characters.name: Medea's Children
characters.description: The two sons of Medea and Jason, killed by Medea as revenge against Jason.

characters.name: Serpent
characters.description: A serpent in Greek mythology, often associated with transformation or guardianship.

characters.name: Colchian Dragon
characters.description: The serpent / dragon that guarded the Golden Fleece in Colchis.

characters.name: Armenius
characters.description: Father of Er, the Pamphylian who returned from the dead in Plato's myth.

characters.name: Greeks
characters.description: The Greek people, also called Achaeans or Danaans in Homer.

characters.name: Boar
characters.description: A wild boar; killed Idmon the seer among the Mariandyni.

characters.name: Bull
characters.description: A bull, often associated with Poseidon and appearing in myths of Crete.

characters.name: Swan
characters.description: A bird associated with transformation in Greek mythology.

myths.name: Abduction of Oreithyia
myths.summary: Boreas, the north wind, carried off Oreithyia while she was playing by the stream of Ilissus. An altar to Boreas marks the spot.

myths.name: Oedipus
myths.summary: Oedipus kills his father Laius and marries his mother Jocasta, fulfilling a prophecy. The story is used by Freud to illustrate the Oedipus complex.

myths.name: Ixion and the Centaurs
myths.summary: Myth of Ixion and the centaurs, used as an example of allegorical interpretation.

myths.name: Minotaur
myths.summary: Legend of the Minotaur, dealing with persistent human fears and emotions.

myths.name: House of Atreus
myths.summary: Saga of the House of Atreus, dealing with persistent human fears and emotions.

myths.name: Apollo and Daphne
myths.summary: Apollo pursues Daphne, who is transformed to escape him. The story is the first love story in Ovid's Metamorphoses.

myths.name: Hippolytus and Phaedra
myths.summary: Hippolytus defines chastity and Phaedra defines lust, reversing typical gender roles.

myths.name: Io and Zeus
myths.summary: Zeus takes Io by force, or their son Epaphus is born by the touch of Zeus's hand.

myths.name: Eos and Cephalus
myths.summary: Eos relentlessly pursues Cephalus, who succumbs to the goddess.

myths.name: Eos and Tithonus
myths.summary: Eos relentlessly pursues Tithonus, who succumbs to the goddess.

myths.name: Salmacis and Hermaphroditus
myths.summary: Salmacis attacks innocent Hermaphroditus and wins.

myths.name: Seduction of Anchises
myths.summary: Aphrodite seduces Anchises, who cannot resist her guile.

myths.name: Hylas and the Nymphs
myths.summary: Beautiful nymphs in a pool are enamored of Hylas and drag him down into the depths.

myths.name: Abduction of Helen
myths.summary: Paris woos Helen, who falls in love and goes willingly to Troy, though some versions depict force.

myths.name: Abduction of Persephone
myths.summary: Hades brutally abducts Persephone to be queen of the Underworld, with Zeus's approval, but Demeter and Persephone disagree.

myths.name: Zeus and Ganymede
myths.summary: Zeus, the king of the gods, falls in love with the young mortal Ganymede and takes him as a lover, a myth that exemplifies male homosexual relationships in classical mythology.

myths.name: Poseidon and Pelops
myths.summary: Poseidon, god of the sea, engages in a male homosexual relationship with the mortal Pelops.

myths.name: Apollo and Hyacinthus
myths.summary: Apollo loves the young man Hyacinthus, but Hyacinthus dies accidentally; from his blood Apollo creates the hyacinth flower.

myths.name: Apollo and Cyparissus
myths.summary: Apollo loves the youth Cyparissus, who is transformed into a cypress tree after grieving over a slain stag.

myths.name: Achilles and Patroclus
myths.summary: The deep bond between the Greek heroes Achilles and Patroclus is a central theme of the Iliad, often interpreted as a homosexual relationship.

myths.name: Orestes and Pylades
myths.summary: The friendship between Orestes and Pylades, especially in Euripides' Iphigenia in Tauris, is a major theme of male homosexuality.

myths.name: Heracles and Hylas
myths.summary: Heracles loves the young Hylas, who is abducted by nymphs during the Argonautic expedition.

myths.name: Nisus and Euryalus
myths.summary: In Roman legend, the love and devotion between Nisus and Euryalus is a moving example of male homosexuality.

myths.name: Minotaur and Labyrinth
myths.summary: The labyrinth at Cnossus housed the Minotaur, a monster half-bull and half-human. Theseus, an Athenian hero, entered the labyrinth and slew the Minotaur, freeing Athens from tribute to Crete.

myths.name: Atlantis
myths.summary: A legendary island culture that vanished into the sea after a conflict with Attica, recorded by Plato in Critias and Timaeus. Possibly reflects the destruction of Thera or Crete.

myths.name: Trojan War
myths.summary: Legendary war between Greeks and Trojans, traditionally dated around 1184 B.C. for the fall of Troy. The war is described in Homer's Iliad and involved heroes like Agamemnon, Priam, and Aeneas. Archaeological evidence from Troy VI and VIIa suggests a historical conflict around 1250-1150 B.C.

myths.name: Odyssey
myths.summary: The epic poem by Homer recounting the ten-year journey of Odysseus home after the Trojan War, including his encounters with mythical creatures and the eventual slaying of Penelope's suitors.

myths.name: Iliad
myths.summary: Epic poem attributed to Homer, focusing on the Trojan War and the hero Achilles, containing the catalogue of ships which preserves Mycenaean historical detail.

myths.name: Cadmus and the founding of Thebes
myths.summary: Legend of Cadmus, who taught writing to the natives of Thebes, likely referring to Mycenaean Linear B.

myths.name: Hesiod's Theogony
myths.summary: Hesiod's account of the creation of the gods, universe, and humankind, beginning with Chaos and proceeding through the generations of gods leading to Zeus's supremacy.

myths.name: Aristophanes' Birds
myths.summary: A comedic account of creation by the playwright Aristophanes, where Night lays an egg from which Eros hatches, leading to the mingling of all things and the birth of the gods.

myths.name: Ovid's Metamorphoses
myths.summary: Ovid's Roman version of creation, where Chaos is a crude unformed mass from which a god or higher nature forms the ordered universe, emphasizing the four elements.

myths.name: Sacred Marriage of Uranus and Gaia
myths.summary: Gaia brings forth Uranus to cover her, and together they produce offspring; Gaia also bears mountains and Pontus without union.

myths.name: Orphic creation
myths.summary: A myth associated with Orpheus and Orphism, featuring the world-egg and Eros as Phanes/Protogonus who brings light and creation.

myths.name: Sacred Marriage
myths.summary: The union of Uranus (Sky) and Gaia (Earth) represents the hieros gamos, a recurring theme in mythology where sky and earth deities mate to produce offspring.

myths.name: Birth of Titans
myths.summary: Gaia and Uranus produce twelve Titans: Oceanus, Coeus, Crius, Hyperion, Iapetus, Theia, Rhea, Themis, Mnemosyne, Phoebe, Tethys, and Cronus.

myths.name: Birth of Cyclopes
myths.summary: Gaia and Uranus produce the Cyclopes: Brontes, Steropes, and Arges, who have one eye in the middle of their foreheads and later fashion Zeus's thunderbolt.

myths.name: Birth of Hecatonchires
myths.summary: Gaia and Uranus produce three hundred-armed, fifty-headed sons: Cottus, Briareus, and Gyes, who are hated by their father.

myths.name: Oceanids
myths.summary: Oceanus and Tethys produce numerous children, the Oceanids: three thousand daughters and three thousand sons, spirits of rivers, waters, and springs.

myths.name: Hyperion and Helius
myths.summary: Hyperion, a Titan sun-god, mates with Theia (or Euryphaëssa) to produce Helius (sun), Selene (moon), and Eos (dawn). Helius drives a chariot across the sky.

myths.name: Phaëthon
myths.summary: Phaëthon, son of Helius and Clymene, is challenged about his parentage and seeks confirmation from his father the Sun.

myths.name: Leucothoë
myths.summary: Helius loves Leucothoë, daughter of Orchamus. Disguised as her mother, he seduces her. Clytië, jealous, reveals the affair, and Orchamus buries Leucothoë alive. Helius turns her corpse into a frankincense tree.

myths.name: Clytië
myths.summary: Clytië, an Oceanid, loves Helius but is rejected after betraying Leucothoë. She pines away, watching the sun, and turns into a sunflower.

myths.name: Rhodes
myths.summary: When Zeus divided the world, Helius was absent, but he claimed the island of Rhodes when it rose from the sea. He loved the nymph Rhode, and their descendants founded the cities of Rhodes.

myths.name: Endymion
myths.summary: Selene loves the shepherd Endymion, who sleeps eternally on Mount Latmus. Zeus grants him perpetual sleep and youth, either as a punishment or to fulfill Selene's wish.

myths.name: Pandia
myths.summary: Zeus and Selene unite, and Selene bears a daughter, Pandia, who is exceptionally lovely.

myths.name: Tithonus
myths.summary: Eos asks Zeus to make Tithonus immortal but forgets to ask for eternal youth. Tithonus ages eternally, eventually becoming a grasshopper.

myths.name: Castration of Uranus
myths.summary: Uranus hides his children in Earth. Ge plots revenge and gives Cronus a sickle. Cronus castrates Uranus, and from the blood spring the Erinyes, Giants, and Meliae. From the foam of the genitals in the sea, Aphrodite is born.

myths.name: Birth of Aphrodite
myths.summary: Aphrodite is born from the foam of Uranus' severed genitals. She first lands at Cythera, then Cyprus. Eros and Desire attend her.

myths.name: Birth of Zeus
myths.summary: Cronus swallowed his children to prevent a prophecy that he would be overthrown by his son. Rhea, with help from Gaea and Uranus, hid Zeus in Crete and gave Cronus a stone wrapped in swaddling clothes to swallow instead. Zeus was raised in a cave on Mount Dicte or Mount Ida.

myths.name: Overthrow of Cronus
myths.summary: Cronus, having swallowed his children, was later overthrown by his son Zeus, who forced him to disgorge the other gods. Cronus was then deposed and retired to the Islands of the Blessed.

myths.name: Creation Myth
myths.summary: Hesiod's Theogony describes the origins of the universe from Chaos, the birth of Gaia and Uranus, and the succession myth involving castration of Uranus by Cronus.

myths.name: Titanomachy
myths.summary: Zeus and his siblings, freed from Cronus, wage a ten-year war against Cronus and the Titans. With the help of the Hecatonchires and Cyclopes, Zeus defeats the Titans and imprisons them in Tartarus. Atlas is punished to hold up the sky.

myths.name: Gigantomachy
myths.summary: Earth (Ge) produces giants and Typhoeus to challenge Zeus. Zeus defeats the giants with the help of Heracles and imprisons them under the earth. Typhoeus, a hundred-headed dragon, is hurled into Tartarus after a fierce battle.

myths.name: Creation of Mortals
myths.summary: Mortals are created by Prometheus, who fashions them from clay and water, and Athena breathes life into them. Ovid describes man as a superior creature with a lofty visage, able to look up to the sky.

myths.name: The Five Ages of Man
myths.summary: Hesiod describes five successive ages of humanity: Gold (under Cronus, carefree), Silver (foolish, destroyed by Zeus), Bronze (warlike, self-destroyed), Heroes (demigods who fought at Thebes and Troy, some sent to Islands of the Blessed), and Iron (current age of toil, wickedness, and eventual destruction by Zeus).

myths.name: Prometheus against Zeus
myths.summary: Prometheus, son of Iapetus, tricks Zeus at Mecone by dividing an ox unfairly. In retaliation, Zeus binds Prometheus and sends an eagle to eat his liver daily, which regenerates nightly. Heracles later kills the eagle and frees Prometheus, with Zeus's consent, to increase Heracles' fame.

myths.name: The Trick at Mecone
myths.summary: Prometheus tricks Zeus by dividing a sacrificial ox into two portions: one with flesh and innards wrapped in paunch, the other with bones wrapped in fat. Zeus chooses the bones, establishing the practice of burning bones for the gods.

myths.name: The Theft of Fire
myths.summary: After Zeus hides fire from mortals in anger at Prometheus' trick, Prometheus steals fire in a hollow fennel stalk and gives it to humans, angering Zeus further.

myths.name: The Creation of Pandora
myths.summary: As punishment for Prometheus' theft of fire, Zeus orders Hephaestus to create the first woman, Pandora, who is adorned by Athena and other gods. She is given to Epimetheus and brings a jar containing evils and hope; when opened, evils escape into the world, leaving only hope inside.

myths.name: Prometheus Bound
myths.summary: In Aeschylus' play, Prometheus is bound as punishment for giving fire to mortals. He claims to have given humans blind hopes to prevent them from foreseeing their fate.

myths.name: Lycaon
myths.summary: Zeus (Jupiter) tests the wickedness of mortals in the Iron Age by becoming a man. He is angered by the evil of Lycaon and punishes him, leading to the decision to send a great flood.

myths.name: Flood of Deucalion
myths.summary: Zeus sends a great flood to punish mortals for their wickedness. Deucalion, son of Prometheus, and Pyrrha, daughter of Epimetheus, survive and repopulate the earth.

myths.name: The Flood
myths.summary: Jupiter decides to destroy humanity with a great flood instead of fire; Neptune aids by sending waves; only Deucalion and Pyrrha survive on Mount Parnassus.

myths.name: Deucalion and Pyrrha
myths.summary: After the flood, Deucalion and Pyrrha consult Themis, who tells them to throw the bones of their mother (stones) behind them; the stones turn into humans, repopulating the earth.

myths.name: Zeus' Rise to Power
myths.summary: Zeus overthrows his father Cronus and the Titans, defeats the Giants and Prometheus, and slays the dragon Typhoeus to become supreme god.

myths.name: Battle with Typhoeus
myths.summary: Zeus kills the dragon Typhoeus, establishing himself as the archetypal dragonslayer.

myths.name: Enuma Elish
myths.summary: Babylonian creation epic where Marduk defeats Tiamat, splits her body to create the sky and earth, and creates humans from the blood of Kingu.

myths.name: Atrahasis
myths.summary: Babylonian myth where Enlil creates humans to serve the gods, then sends a flood to destroy them, but Atrahasis survives with Enki's help.

myths.name: Epic of Gilgamesh
myths.summary: Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, and his friend Enkidu kill Humbaba and the Bull of Heaven; after Enkidu's death, Gilgamesh seeks immortality and meets Ut-napishtim.

myths.name: Flood
myths.summary: A great flood sent by Enlil to destroy humanity; survivors include Atrahasis, Ut-napishtim, Deucalion, and Noah.

myths.name: Sacred Marriage of Zeus and Hera
myths.summary: Zeus and Hera enact the sacred marriage between sky-god and earth-goddess, described in Homer's Iliad where the earth sprouts new grass and flowers as they lie together under a golden cloud.

myths.name: Binding of Zeus
myths.summary: Hera, Poseidon, and Athena once bound Zeus in chains, but Thetis rescued him. This event is alluded to in the Iliad.

myths.name: Rape of Persephone
myths.summary: Demeter's daughter Persephone was abducted by Hades, causing Demeter to grieve and refuse to let the earth bear fruit until Persephone was returned.

myths.name: Homeric Hymn to Hestia (24)
myths.summary: A brief hymn calling on Hestia as the personification of the protecting flame of the sacred hearth in a temple, asking her to enter the house with Zeus and grant grace to the song.

myths.name: Homeric Hymn to Hestia (29)
myths.summary: A hymn invoking Hestia as protectress of the hearth in the home, along with Hermes, asking them to inhabit beautiful homes in loving harmony.

myths.name: Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite
myths.summary: Aphrodite proclaims she is the greatest deity, able to bend even Zeus to her amorous will, except for Athena, Artemis, and Hestia who defy her.

myths.name: Founding of Olympic Games
myths.summary: Heracles was said to have founded the original Olympic Games, which were reorganized in 776 BCE with Zeus as principal god.

myths.name: Battle of Centaurs and Lapiths
myths.summary: At the wedding of Pirithoüs and Hippodamia, centaurs got drunk and attempted to carry off the bride and other Lapith women, leading to a battle. The myth was depicted on the west pediment of the temple of Zeus at Olympia and in the metopes of the Parthenon.

myths.name: Chariot Race of Pelops and Hippodamia
myths.summary: Pelops competed in a chariot race against Oenomaüs to win Hippodamia as his wife. The scene before the race is depicted on the east pediment of the temple of Zeus at Olympia, with Zeus as central figure guaranteeing Pelops' success.

myths.name: Twelve Labors of Heracles
myths.summary: Heracles performed twelve labors, including cleansing the stables of Augeas, capturing the Nemean Lion, and fetching Cerberus. These were carved in the metopes of the temple of Zeus at Olympia, with Athena and Hermes helping in some labors.

myths.name: Killing of Niobe's children
myths.summary: Apollo and Artemis killed the children of Niobe. This myth was depicted on the feet of the throne of Zeus at Olympia.

myths.name: Freeing Prometheus
myths.summary: Heracles freed Prometheus, depicted on the screen enclosing the throne of Zeus at Olympia.

myths.name: Ganymede
myths.summary: Zeus chose the handsome youth Ganymede to be cupbearer on Olympus, granting him immortality. The myth has been interpreted variously as a religious calling, a rape, or a joke.

myths.name: Abduction of Ganymede
myths.summary: Zeus, in the form of a whirlwind or eagle, abducts the handsome Trojan prince Ganymede to be his cupbearer. He compensates Ganymede's father Tros with divine horses and grants Ganymede immortality.

myths.name: Return of Hephaestus to Olympus
myths.summary: Hephaestus, cast out of Olympus by Hera or Zeus, is brought back by Dionysus who makes him drunk. The scene is depicted on vases with Hephaestus on a donkey led by Dionysus and his retinue.

myths.name: Quarrel of Zeus and Hera
myths.summary: Zeus and Hera argue over Zeus's promise to Thetis to honor Achilles. Hephaestus intervenes, reminding them of his own fall from Olympus, and calms Hera by offering her a cup of nectar.

myths.name: Thetis' Supplication
myths.summary: Thetis, mother of Achilles, supplicates Zeus to grant victory to the Trojans until the Greeks honor her son. Zeus agrees, nodding his head, which causes Olympus to tremble.

myths.name: Shield of Achilles
myths.summary: Hephaestus creates an elaborate shield for Achilles, described in detail in Homer's Iliad.

myths.name: The Love Affair of Ares and Aphrodite
myths.summary: Hephaestus, learning from Helius that his wife Aphrodite is having an affair with Ares, forges an unbreakable net to trap them in bed. He summons the other gods to witness their shame, but Poseidon persuades him to release them. Ares flees to Thrace, and Aphrodite goes to Paphos where the Graces attend to her.

myths.name: Homeric Hymn to the Muses and Apollo
myths.summary: A hymn invoking the Muses and Apollo, stating that through them humans become poets and musicians, and through Zeus they become kings. The Muses are praised as children of Zeus.

myths.name: Homeric Hymn to the Supreme Son of Cronus
myths.summary: A hymn to Zeus, the best and greatest of gods, who confides his words of wisdom to Themis. It emphasizes Zeus's role as ruler and accomplisher.

myths.name: Story of the Daughters of Pierus
myths.summary: Nine daughters of Pierus challenged the Muses to a musical contest, lost, and were turned into magpies.

myths.name: Story of Trophonius and Agamedes
myths.summary: Trophonius and Agamedes built the temple of Apollo at Delphi. When they asked for wages, Apollo said he would pay on the seventh day, and they fell asleep forever.

myths.name: Story of Cleobis and Biton
myths.summary: Cleobis and Biton, Argive brothers, died peacefully after a life of piety, similar to the story of Trophonius and Agamedes.

myths.name: The Meeting Between Solon and Croesus
myths.summary: Solon visits Croesus and tells him that Tellus the Athenian is the happiest person, followed by Cleobis and Biton, who died peacefully after honoring their mother. Solon warns Croesus that wealth does not guarantee happiness until life ends well.

myths.name: The Death of Atys
myths.summary: Croesus' son Atys dies, fulfilling a prophecy despite Croesus' attempts to avoid it. The story illustrates the interplay of fate and character.

myths.name: The Tragedy of Croesus
myths.summary: Croesus, king of Lydia, is visited by Solon who warns him not to call anyone happy until death. Croesus ignores this. His son Atys is killed accidentally by Adrastus during a boar hunt, fulfilling a dream prophecy. Later, Croesus attacks Persia based on an ambiguous Delphic oracle, leading to his downfall. He is captured by Cyrus and placed on a pyre, but calls out Solon's name, prompting Cyrus to spare him.

myths.name: Tragedy of Croesus
myths.summary: Croesus, king of Lydia, learns from Solon that no man can be called happy until dead. He later attacks Persia, is captured by Cyrus, and is saved from burning by Apollo. He becomes Cyrus's counselor.

myths.name: Gyges and Candaules
myths.summary: King Candaules of Lydia forces his bodyguard Gyges to see his wife naked. The wife, insulted, forces Gyges to kill Candaules and marry her, making Gyges king.

myths.name: Arion and the Dolphin
myths.summary: The musician Arion, thrown overboard by sailors, is saved by a dolphin that carries him to safety. He later confronts the sailors with Periander.

myths.name: Polycrates' Ring
myths.summary: Polycrates, tyrant of Samos, throws his prized ring into the sea to avoid divine jealousy, but it is returned in a fish. His friend Amasis realizes his fate is sealed, and Polycrates is later murdered.

myths.name: Panathenaic Festival
myths.summary: Annual festival honoring Athena Polias, involving a procession, presentation of a peplos embroidered with the Gigantomachy, sacrifice, and artistic representations on the Parthenon.

myths.name: Orestes' arrival in Athens
myths.summary: Orestes arrived in Athens after killing his mother; this myth was recalled during the Anthesteria festival.

myths.name: Killing and dismemberment of Dionysus
myths.summary: Dionysus was killed and dismembered; this myth was recalled during the Anthesteria festival.

myths.name: Legend of Icarius and Erigone
myths.summary: Icarius and his daughter Erigone were involved in a myth recalled during the Anthesteria festival.

myths.name: Peleus and Thetis
myths.summary: Thetis was destined to bear a son mightier than his father, so Zeus avoided her. She married mortal Peleus, who caught her despite her shape-shifting. Their son Achilles became mightier than Peleus.

myths.name: Acis, Galatea, and the Cyclops Polyphemus
myths.summary: The Cyclops Polyphemus loved the Nereid Galatea, but she loved Acis. Polyphemus killed Acis by throwing a rock, but Galatea transformed Acis into a river-god.

myths.name: Poseidon and Amphitrite
myths.summary: Poseidon won Amphitrite as his wife after she initially resisted. They had a son Triton. Poseidon had affairs, causing Amphitrite's jealousy.

myths.name: Tyro and Poseidon
myths.summary: Poseidon disguised himself as the river Enipeus and lay with Tyro, resulting in twins Neleus and Pelias.

myths.name: Proteus and Menelaüs
myths.summary: Menelaüs, with help from Proteus' daughter Eidothea, consulted Proteus. Proteus changed shape but eventually answered Menelaüs' questions about his return home.

myths.name: Scylla and Charybdis
myths.summary: Scylla was transformed into a monster due to Amphitrite's or Circe's jealousy. She and Charybdis, a voracious daughter of Poseidon and Ge, terrorized the Straits of Messina.

myths.name: Progeny of Pontus and Ge
myths.summary: Pontus and Ge produced Nereus, Thaumas, Phorcys, Ceto, and Eurybië. Their descendants include many sea deities and monsters.

myths.name: Contest for Athens
myths.summary: Poseidon and Athena competed for control of Athens and Attica. The story is associated with the west pediment of the Parthenon.

myths.name: Galatea and Acis
myths.summary: Galatea, a sea nymph, spurned the love of the Cyclops Polyphemus for the youth Acis. Polyphemus caught them together and crushed Acis under a rock, but Galatea transformed his blood into a river, making him a river-god.

myths.name: Neptune and Amphitrite
myths.summary: Amphitrite, daughter of Nereus, initially spurned Neptune's advances but eventually became his consort. Poussin's painting depicts their triumph.

myths.name: Perseus and Medusa
myths.summary: The hero Perseus beheaded the Gorgon Medusa, who was pregnant by Poseidon. From her corpse sprang Pegasus and Chrysaor.

myths.name: Heracles and the Apples of the Hesperides
myths.summary: Heracles slew the dragon Ladon to steal the golden apples guarded by the Hesperides.

myths.name: Heracles and Geryon
myths.summary: Heracles overcame the monster Geryon and his hound Orthus.

myths.name: Heracles and the Hydra
myths.summary: Heracles slew the Lernaean Hydra, a monster offspring of Echidna and Typhon.

myths.name: Heracles and the Nemean Lion
myths.summary: Heracles killed the Nemean Lion, a monster offspring of Echidna and Orthus.

myths.name: Birth of Athena
myths.summary: Athena was born from the head of Zeus, fully armed, after Zeus swallowed her mother Metis. Hephaestus (or Prometheus or Hermes) assisted by splitting Zeus's head. The event caused awe among the gods and cosmic disturbances.

myths.name: Contest with Poseidon for Athens
myths.summary: Athena and Poseidon competed for control of Athens. Athena produced an olive tree with her spear, while Poseidon created a salt spring (or horse). Athena was declared victor by the gods, Athenians, or King Cecrops. Poseidon flooded the Thriasian plain in anger but was appeased.

myths.name: Pallas and Athena
myths.summary: Athena was reared by Triton and had a playmate named Pallas. During a quarrel, Zeus intervened with the aegis, startling Pallas, and Athena accidentally killed her. In grief, Athena made a wooden image (the Palladium) which fell to Troy.

myths.name: Athena and Arachne
myths.summary: Arachne, a mortal weaver, boasted that her skill equaled Athena's. Athena (as Minerva) challenged her to a contest. Arachne wove a tapestry depicting the Rape of Europa, angering Athena, who struck her with a shuttle.

myths.name: Amazonomachy
myths.summary: Battle between Greeks and Amazons, depicted on the west metopes of the Parthenon and on the exterior of Athena's shield.

myths.name: Centauromachy
myths.summary: Battle of the Lapiths and centaurs, depicted on the south metopes of the Parthenon and on Athena's sandals.

myths.name: Sack of Troy
myths.summary: The destruction of Troy, depicted on the north metopes of the Parthenon.

myths.name: Arachne
myths.summary: Arachne, a Lydian woman, challenges Athena to a weaving contest. Athena weaves scenes of gods punishing mortals, while Arachne weaves scenes of gods' amorous deceptions. Enraged by Arachne's success, Athena destroys her tapestry and strikes her. Arachne hangs herself, but Athena transforms her into a spider.

myths.name: Oresteia
myths.summary: Athena sides with Apollo for the acquittal of Orestes, creating the court of the Areopagus and appeasing the Furies.

myths.name: Pygmalion
myths.summary: Pygmalion, disgusted by the prostitute women of Cyprus, sculpted an ivory statue of a woman and fell in love with it. He prayed to Venus, who brought the statue to life. They married and had a son, Paphos.

myths.name: Aphrodite and Adonis
myths.summary: Myrrha, daughter of Cinyras, committed incest with her father and was transformed into a myrrh tree, giving birth to Adonis. Aphrodite fell in love with Adonis, but he was killed by a boar while hunting.

myths.name: Cybele and Attis
myths.summary: Cybele, the Great Mother, falls in love with Attis. He loves another, and Cybele drives him mad; he castrates himself and dies. Cybele repents and obtains Zeus' promise that Attis' body will never decay.

myths.name: Aphrodite and Anchises
myths.summary: Zeus causes Aphrodite to fall in love with the mortal Anchises as revenge for her boasts. The Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite describes her power and her union with Anchises, who fears debilitation from sleeping with a goddess.

myths.name: Aristophanes' Speech
myths.summary: In Plato's Symposium, Aristophanes explains that humans originally had three sexes (male, female, and androgynous) and were spherical with four arms and four legs. They attacked the gods, so Zeus split them in half, causing humans to seek their other half. Eros is the desire to reunite with one's original other half.

myths.name: Aristophanes' Speech in the Symposium
myths.summary: Aristophanes explains the origin of love by recounting a myth where humans were originally spherical beings with two faces, four arms, and four legs. Zeus split them in two as punishment for their insolence, and Apollo healed them. Now each half longs for its other half, and love is the desire for wholeness.

myths.name: Socrates' Speech in the Symposium
myths.summary: Socrates, instructed by Diotima, argues that Eros is not a god but a great spirit intermediate between gods and humans. Eros is neither good nor bad, beautiful nor ugly, but a lover of wisdom who seeks the good and the beautiful.

myths.name: Cupid and Psyche
myths.summary: A king and queen have three daughters; the youngest, Psyche, is so beautiful that Venus becomes jealous. Venus orders Cupid to make Psyche fall in love with a monster, but Cupid falls in love with her instead. Psyche is left on a mountaintop as a bride for a serpent, but Zephyrus carries her to Cupid's palace. After trials and labors, she is united with Cupid.

myths.name: Birth of Artemis and Apollo
myths.summary: Leto, impregnated by Zeus, gives birth to the twin deities Artemis and Apollo on the island of Delos. Artemis is born first and helps deliver Apollo. Hera's anger forces Leto to wander; in Lycia, she turns inhospitable Lycians into frogs.

myths.name: Niobe and Her Children
myths.summary: Niobe, queen of Thebes, boasts that she is more deserving of worship than Leto because she has seven sons and seven daughters. Leto complains to Artemis and Apollo, who kill all of Niobe's children with arrows. Niobe is turned to stone and placed on a mountaintop in Phrygia, where she weeps eternally.

myths.name: Actaeon
myths.summary: The hunter Actaeon accidentally stumbles upon Artemis bathing naked in a cave. In anger, Artemis splashes water on him, transforming him into a stag. His own hunting hounds, not recognizing him, chase and tear him apart.

myths.name: Death of Actaeon
myths.summary: Actaeon accidentally sees Artemis bathing; as punishment, she transforms him into a stag, and he is torn apart by his own hounds.

myths.name: Callisto and Arcas
myths.summary: Jupiter seduces Callisto by disguising as Diana; Callisto becomes pregnant and is expelled by Diana; Juno transforms her into a bear; her son Arcas nearly kills her but Jupiter turns them into constellations.

myths.name: Orion
myths.summary: Orion, a mighty hunter, woos Merope, is blinded by Oenopion, regains sight via Helius, attempts to rape Artemis, and is killed by a scorpion sent by her; he and his dog become constellations.

myths.name: Arethusa
myths.summary: The river-god Alpheus pursues the nymph Arethusa; she prays to Artemis, who transforms her into a stream that flows underground to Syracuse.

myths.name: Hippolytus
myths.summary: Aphrodite, angered by Hippolytus' devotion to Artemis and rejection of love, causes his stepmother Phaedra to fall in love with him. Phaedra's nurse reveals the secret to Hippolytus, who is horrified. Phaedra commits suicide and leaves a note falsely accusing Hippolytus of rape. Theseus curses Hippolytus, leading to his death. Artemis appears to the dying Hippolytus, promising vengeance and establishing a cult in his honor.

myths.name: Callisto
myths.summary: Callisto, a follower of Artemis, is seduced by Zeus and transformed into a bear. She becomes the constellation Ursa Major.

myths.name: Niobe
myths.summary: Niobe, wife of Amphion, boasts of her many children, angering Leto, who sends Apollo and Artemis to kill them. Niobe is turned to stone on Mount Sipylus.

myths.name: Birth of Artemis
myths.summary: Artemis is born on Delos (or Ortygia) to Leto and Zeus, assisting in the birth of her twin brother Apollo.

myths.name: Birth of Apollo
myths.summary: Leto, pregnant with Apollo and Artemis, wanders seeking a place to give birth. Delos agrees to accept Apollo after Leto swears an oath that Apollo will build his temple there. After nine days of labor, with the help of Eileithyia, Apollo is born on Delos under a palm tree. Themis feeds him nectar and ambrosia, and Apollo immediately declares his domains: lyre, bow, and prophecy.

myths.name: Apollo and Delos
myths.summary: Delos becomes the sacred island of Apollo, site of his important sanctuary. The Homeric Hymn describes the festival at Delos with the Deliades maidens singing. The story of Anius, son of Apollo, is also associated with Delos.

myths.name: Daughters of Anius
myths.summary: Anius, king of Delos, had three daughters who received from Dionysus the power to produce oil, grain, and wine. Agamemnon tried to force them to go to Troy, but they resisted and were turned into white doves by Dionysus.

myths.name: Hymn to Apollo
myths.summary: The Homeric Hymn to Apollo describes Apollo's descent from Olympus, his journey through Greece, and his foundation of the oracle at Delphi after slaying the she-dragon Python. It also tells how Apollo recruited Cretan sailors as his attendants by transforming into a dolphin.

myths.name: Slaying of the Python
myths.summary: Apollo slew a she-dragon at Crisa near Parnassus, and the site was called Pytho because the sun made the monster rot. This act represents Apollo's conquest of the earlier earth-goddess oracle.

myths.name: Foundation of Delphi
myths.summary: Zeus released two eagles from opposite ends of the earth; they met at Delphi, marking it as the center of the earth. Apollo established his oracle there after slaying the dragon and recruiting Cretan sailors.

myths.name: Apollo and the Cretan Ship
myths.summary: Apollo transformed into a dolphin and leaped aboard a Cretan ship, forcing the sailors to follow him to Crisa. He revealed himself as a god and appointed them as attendants at his sanctuary.

myths.name: Oracle at Delphi
myths.summary: The Pythia, Apollo's prophetess, delivered oracles from the tripod in the adyton. Inquirers underwent purification and sacrifices before consulting the god. The oracle was active nine months a year and was known for ambiguous responses.

myths.name: The Cumaean Sibyl
myths.summary: The Cumaean Sibyl, a prophetess of Apollo, guides Aeneas in the underworld. She prophesies in a cavern with a hundred mouths, and her prophecies are sometimes written on leaves that scatter. Apollo loved her and granted her long life, but she forgot to ask for eternal youth, so she ages and eventually becomes a tiny voice.

myths.name: Apollo and Cassandra
myths.summary: Apollo loved Cassandra, daughter of Priam, and gave her the power of prophecy. When she rejected him, he spat into her mouth, ensuring that no one would ever believe her prophecies.

myths.name: Apollo and Marpessa
myths.summary: Apollo and Idas both wooed Marpessa. Idas carried her off, and Apollo stole her back. Zeus ordered Marpessa to choose; she chose Idas, fearing Apollo would abandon her when she grew old.

myths.name: Apollo and Cyrene
myths.summary: Apollo fell in love with the athletic nymph Cyrene while watching her wrestle a lion. He took her to Libya, where the city Cyrene was named after her, and she bore him a son, Aristaeus.

myths.name: Apollo and Coronis
myths.summary: Apollo loves Coronis, who is pregnant with his child. A raven reports her infidelity; Apollo kills her with an arrow but repents. He saves his son Asclepius from the funeral pyre and gives him to Chiron to raise.

myths.name: Apollo's Musical Contest with Marsyas
myths.summary: Marsyas, a satyr, picked up the flute discarded by Athena and became so proficient that he challenged Apollo to a musical contest. Apollo won and flayed Marsyas alive. The satyr's tears formed the river Marsyas in Phrygia.

myths.name: Apollo's Musical Contest with Pan
myths.summary: Pan challenged Apollo to a musical contest, with Tmolus as judge. Tmolus judged Apollo the winner, but Midas disagreed. Apollo gave Midas ass's ears as punishment. Midas's barber revealed the secret by whispering into a hole, and reeds grew that spread the story.

myths.name: Alcestis
myths.summary: Apollo, in exile for killing the Cyclopes, served King Admetus. He obtained longer life for Admetus from the Moirai on condition that someone die in his place. Admetus's wife Alcestis volunteered, but Heracles rescued her from death by wrestling Thanatos.

myths.name: Asclepius and Hippolytus
myths.summary: Asclepius, a skilled physician, restored Hippolytus to life at Artemis's request. Zeus, angered by this disruption of nature, struck Asclepius with a thunderbolt and hurled him into the underworld.

myths.name: Apollo at Troy
myths.summary: Apollo, angered by the insult to his priest Chryses, descends from Olympus and shoots plague arrows at the Greek camp, causing mass death.

myths.name: Apollo Seeks a Site for His Oracle
myths.summary: Apollo travels over the earth seeking a location for his oracle. He eventually chooses Delphi, where he slays the Python.

myths.name: Homeric Hymn to Apollo
myths.summary: The hymn describes Apollo's arrival at Olympus, where he plays the lyre and the gods dance and sing. It also mentions his love affairs and his search for an oracle site.

myths.name: Apollo and the Python
myths.summary: Apollo slays the serpent Python at Delphi, thereby taking possession of the site for his oracle.

myths.name: Apollo's Search for a Temple Site
myths.summary: Apollo searches for a location to build his temple and oracle. He rejects several sites, is deceived by Telphusa, and finally chooses Crisa beneath Mt. Parnassus, where he builds his temple at Delphi.

myths.name: Slaying of the She-Dragon
myths.summary: Apollo kills the she-dragon at Delphi with his bow. The monster had been raised by Hera and had caused harm to mortals. After her death, the place is called Pytho, and Apollo is titled Pythian.

myths.name: Birth of Typhaon
myths.summary: Angry at Zeus for giving birth to Athena alone, Hera prays to Earth and the Titans for a child stronger than Zeus. She gives birth to Typhaon, a terrible monster, whom she gives to the she-dragon to raise.

myths.name: Recruiting Cretan Priests
myths.summary: Apollo, in the form of a dolphin, leaps onto a Cretan ship and guides it to Crisa. The Cretans become his priests at Delphi.

myths.name: Homeric Hymn to Pythian Apollo
myths.summary: Apollo, in the form of a dolphin, guides a Cretan ship to Crisa, where he establishes his temple at Delphi. He reveals himself as Apollo, son of Zeus, and appoints the Cretans as his priests, instructing them to worship him as Delphinius and to sing the Ie Paean.

myths.name: Apollo and Python
myths.summary: Apollo slew the dragon Python at Delphi, establishing his sanctuary there. The festival Stepteria commemorated this event every ninth year.

myths.name: Apollo and Marsyas
myths.summary: The satyr Marsyas challenged Apollo to a musical contest. After Apollo won, he flayed Marsyas alive for his hubris.

myths.name: Birth and Childhood of Hermes
myths.summary: Zeus fathers Hermes with Maia in a cave, without the knowledge of Hera. Hermes is born on the fourth day of the month and quickly shows his cleverness.

myths.name: Hermes Invents the Lyre
myths.summary: Shortly after birth, Hermes finds a tortoise, kills it, and fashions the first lyre from its shell, using reeds, oxhide, and sheep gut strings. He sings of Zeus and Maia.

myths.name: Hermes Steals Apollo's Cattle
myths.summary: Hermes steals fifty cattle from Apollo, reversing their tracks to confuse pursuit. He invents fire sticks, sacrifices two cows, and hides the meat. He returns to his cradle and confronts his mother Maia, vowing to gain honor.

myths.name: The Cattle of Apollo
myths.summary: Hermes steals fifty cows from Apollo's herd, driving them backward to confuse pursuit. He hides them in a cave near Pylos. Apollo, with the help of an old man and a bird omen, tracks Hermes to his cave. After a dispute, Zeus reconciles them, and Hermes gives Apollo the lyre in exchange for the cattle.

myths.name: The Hymn to Hermes
myths.summary: A Homeric hymn that tells the story of Hermes' birth, his invention of the lyre, theft of Apollo's cattle, and reconciliation with Apollo. It highlights Hermes' cleverness and the establishment of his roles as messenger, god of herds, and guide to the underworld.

myths.name: Homeric Hymn to Hermes
myths.summary: The Homeric Hymn to Hermes describes the birth and early exploits of Hermes, including his theft of Apollo's cattle and invention of the lyre.

myths.name: Hermaphroditus and Salmacis
myths.summary: The nymph Salmacis falls in love with Hermaphroditus, son of Hermes and Aphrodite. When he rejects her, she prays to be united with him forever, and their bodies merge into one being with both male and female attributes.

myths.name: Birth of Dionysus
myths.summary: Zeus had an affair with Semele, a daughter of Cadmus. Hera, jealous, tricked Semele into asking Zeus to appear in his divine form, which killed her. Zeus saved the unborn Dionysus and sewed him into his thigh, from which he was later born. Hermes took the infant to the nymphs of Nysa to be raised.

myths.name: The Bacchae
