myths.summary: Dionysus returns to Thebes to establish his worship and punish his mother's sisters for denying his divinity. He drives the women of Thebes mad, including his aunts, and confronts King Pentheus, who opposes him. The play explores the power and terror of Dionysian worship.

myths.name: Marriage of Dionysus and Ariadne
myths.summary: Dionysus danced with Ariadne, kissed her, and they embraced. The audience watched excitedly as they kissed and moved off to their marriage bed, inspiring others to marry.

myths.name: Daughters of Proetus
myths.summary: The daughters of King Proetus of Tiryns resisted Dionysus and were driven mad, rushing over the countryside and killing their children. The seer Melampus cured them with herbs and therapeutic dances, though one daughter, Iphinoë, died during the pursuit.

myths.name: Daughters of Minyas
myths.summary: The daughters of Minyas of Orchomenus refused to participate in Bacchic worship and were driven mad. Leucippe's son Hippasus was torn to pieces. The Minyads were transformed into winged creatures of the night (owls or bats).

myths.name: Lycurgus
myths.summary: Lycurgus of Thrace pursued the nurses of Dionysus with an ox goad. Dionysus jumped into the sea in terror and was rescued by Thetis. Zeus struck Lycurgus with blindness and he died soon after.

myths.name: Homeric Hymn to Dionysus (1)
myths.summary: A hymn describing the birth of Dionysus, sewn in Zeus' thigh, born on Mount Nysa near Egypt. It establishes the universal power of his worship and triennial festivals.

myths.name: Homeric Hymn to Dionysus (26)
myths.summary: A hymn describing Dionysus as ivy-crowned and loud-crying, nurtured by nymphs in the vales of Mount Nysa. He wanders in the forest with nymphs following him.

myths.name: Silenus and Midas
myths.summary: Silenus, made drunk by wine-laced water, was brought to King Midas. He philosophized that the best fate for humans is not to be born, and the next best is to die soon after birth.

myths.name: Dionysus and Ariadne
myths.summary: Dionysus married Ariadne after she was deserted by Theseus on Naxos, symbolizing the union of male and female vegetation powers and Dionysus' redemptive power.

myths.name: Birth of Zagreus
myths.summary: Zeus mated with Persephone, who bore Zagreus (Dionysus). Hera aroused the Titans to attack the child; they dismembered and devoured him. Athena saved his heart, and Zeus destroyed the Titans with thunder. From the Titans' ashes, humans were born, giving them a dual nature: evil body from Titans, divine soul from the devoured god.

myths.name: Dionysus, Icarius, and Erigone
myths.summary: Icarius was hospitable to Dionysus and received wine as a gift. People thought they were poisoned and killed Icarius. His daughter Erigone searched for him and hanged herself. Plague ensued until, on Apollo's advice, a festival was initiated in their honor.

myths.name: Midas and the Golden Touch
myths.summary: Silenus was captured and brought to King Midas, who returned him to Dionysus. As a reward, Midas was granted the golden touch. He soon regretted it when he could not eat or drink. Dionysus ordered him to wash in the river Pactolus, which then had golden sands.

myths.name: Dionysus and the Pirates
myths.summary: Pirates abducted Dionysus, mistaking him for a mortal. Miracles occurred: wine flowed, vines grew, and the god transformed into a lion and bear. The pirates jumped into the sea and became dolphins. The helmsman was saved.

myths.name: Pan and Syrinx
myths.summary: Pan pursued the nymph Syrinx, who was transformed into marsh reeds. The wind blowing through the reeds produced a sound, inspiring Pan to create the panpipe.

myths.name: Pan and Echo
myths.summary: Pan loved the nymph Echo, but she fled from him. Pan caused madness among shepherds, who tore Echo to pieces. Only her voice remained.

myths.name: Birth of Pan
myths.summary: Pan was born to Hermes and Dryope, daughter of Dryops. He is goat-footed, two-horned, and loves music.

myths.name: Echo and Narcissus
myths.summary: Echo, cursed by Juno to only repeat words, fell in love with Narcissus but was rejected. Narcissus then fell in love with his own reflection in a pool and wasted away, eventually dying. The story includes the prophecy of Tiresias and the prayer of a scorned lover answered by Nemesis.

myths.name: Narcissus and Echo
myths.summary: Narcissus, a beautiful youth, rejected the love of the nymph Echo, who pined away until only her voice remained. As punishment, Narcissus fell in love with his own reflection in a pool, and unable to attain it, he died and was transformed into a flower.

myths.name: The Abduction of Persephone
myths.summary: Persephone is abducted by Hades while picking flowers in a meadow, with Zeus's consent. Demeter searches for her, learns the truth from Helius, and in grief withdraws from the gods, causing the earth to become barren.

myths.name: Demeter at Eleusis
myths.summary: Demeter, disguised as an old woman, comes to Eleusis and is taken in by the family of King Celeus. She becomes nurse to their baby son, but her identity is eventually revealed.

myths.name: Demeter Nurses Demophoön
myths.summary: Demeter, disguised as a nurse, anoints Demophoön with ambrosia and places him in the fire at night to make him immortal. Metaneira interrupts, causing Demeter to reveal herself and stop the process.

myths.name: The Return of Persephone
myths.summary: Zeus sends Hermes to retrieve Persephone from Hades. Hades allows her to leave but tricks her into eating pomegranate seeds, ensuring her return each year. Demeter and Persephone are reunited, and the earth becomes fertile again.

myths.name: The Eleusinian Mysteries
myths.summary: After restoring fertility, Demeter teaches her sacred rites to the kings of Eleusis, including Triptolemus, establishing the Eleusinian Mysteries. Initiates who witness these rites are promised a blessed afterlife.

myths.name: Hymn to Demeter
myths.summary: The Homeric Hymn to Demeter recounts the abduction of Persephone by Hades, Demeter's grief and wanderings, her stay at Eleusis, and the eventual reunion with her daughter, which restores fertility to the earth.

myths.name: Eleusinian Mysteries
myths.summary: The Eleusinian Mysteries were secret religious rites held annually at Eleusis, involving initiation stages (Lesser and Greater Mysteries), processions, purification, and a dramatic reenactment of Demeter's story, culminating in the revelation of sacred objects.

myths.name: Orphic myth of Zagreus
myths.summary: Myth of Zagreus-Dionysus, son of Persephone, who was dismembered and reborn, providing authority for Orphism.

myths.name: Odysseus' Visit to the Underworld
myths.summary: Odysseus travels to the Underworld to consult the seer Tiresias about his return to Ithaca. He performs sacrifices, speaks with the shades of the dead including his mother Anticlea, and encounters heroes like Achilles and Ajax.

myths.name: Odyssey Book 11
myths.summary: Odysseus visits the Underworld, where he sees the souls of the dead, including Minos, Orion, Tityus, Tantalus, Sisyphus, and Heracles. He also encounters his mother Anticlea and heroes like Agamemnon and Achilles.

myths.name: Sisyphus myth
myths.summary: Sisyphus, son of Aeolus, outwits Death by chaining him, preventing mortals from dying. After Ares frees Death, Sisyphus tricks Hades by instructing his wife not to make sacrifices, allowing him to return to Corinth. He is eventually punished in the Underworld by rolling a rock uphill forever.

myths.name: Myth of Er
myths.summary: Er, a Pamphylian, dies in war and returns to life after twelve days. He describes the afterlife: souls are judged and travel through openings in earth and sky, undergoing a thousand-year cycle of punishment and reward.

myths.name: Orpheus myth
myths.summary: Orpheus visits the Underworld to retrieve his wife Eurydice, playing music before Pluto and Proserpina.

myths.name: Heracles' labors
myths.summary: Heracles captures Cerberus, the three-headed dog guarding the Underworld, as one of his labors.

myths.name: Aeneid
myths.summary: Aeneas, guided by the Sibyl, visits the Underworld with the golden bough.

myths.name: Inferno
myths.summary: Dante's epic poem describing a journey through Hell, combining classical myths with medieval Christian doctrine.

myths.name: Aeneas in the Underworld
myths.summary: Aeneas, guided by the Sibyl, descends to the Underworld to visit his father. He must obtain the golden bough and bury Misenus. They encounter various monsters, cross the Styx with Charon, and see unburied souls like Palinurus.

myths.name: Aeneas' Descent to the Underworld
myths.summary: Aeneas, guided by the Sibyl, descends to the Underworld to visit his father Anchises. They encounter Charon, Cerberus, various souls, and the realms of Tartarus and Elysium, witnessing punishments and rewards.

myths.name: Punishment of Ixion
myths.summary: Ixion, son of Phlegyas, killed his father-in-law Eïoneus and was purified by Zeus. He then attempted to violate Hera, but Zeus deceived him with a cloud (Nephele), who bore Centaurus. Ixion was punished by being bound to a winged wheel that rolls eternally.

myths.name: The Frogs
myths.summary: Aristophanes' comedy in which Dionysus rows across the Styx to the Underworld, accompanied by a chorus of frogs croaking 'brekekekex koax koax'. It is a humorous tour of the Underworld.

myths.name: Dialogues of the Dead
myths.summary: Satirical dialogues by Lucian that portray the Underworld in varied moods.

myths.name: Orpheus and Eurydice
myths.summary: Orpheus marries Eurydice, but she dies from a snake bite. Orpheus descends to the underworld and charms Hades and Persephone with his music, winning permission to bring Eurydice back on condition he not look back until they reach the upper world. He fails and loses her forever.

myths.name: Dismemberment of Orpheus
myths.summary: After losing Eurydice, Orpheus shuns women and turns to love of young men. Ciconian maenads, angered by his rejection, attack him during a Bacchic frenzy, tearing him apart. His head and lyre float down the river Hebrus to Lesbos, where Apollo turns a snake to stone. His shade reunites with Eurydice in the underworld.

myths.name: Argonautic expedition
myths.summary: Orpheus was a member of Jason's expedition to retrieve the Golden Fleece.

myths.name: Death of Orpheus
myths.summary: Orpheus is killed by Thracian women, either because he neglected them, refused to initiate them, or enticed their husbands away. In some versions, he is struck by Zeus' thunderbolt or killed by followers of Dionysus. His head and lyre are taken to Lesbos, where his head becomes an oracle.

myths.name: Orphic theogony
myths.summary: The Orphic creation myth begins with Chronus (Time) and Adrasteia (Necessity). From Chronus comes Aether, Chaos, and Erebus. An egg is formed from which Phanes emerges. Phanes creates Night, who bears Gaea and Uranus. Cronus succeeds, then Zeus. Zeus swallows Phanes and recreates everything. Zeus mates with Persephone to produce Dionysus.

myths.name: Mithras Killing the Bull
myths.summary: Mithras slays a bull, from whose blood springs fertility; central to Mithraic iconography.

myths.name: Isis and Osiris
myths.summary: Isis searches for her husband/brother Osiris, dismembered by Seth, and for her child Horus.

myths.name: Lucius and Isis
myths.summary: Lucius, transformed into a donkey, prays to Isis; she appears in a dream and instructs him to take a garland of roses from a priest, restoring his human form.

myths.name: Founding of Thebes
myths.summary: Cadmus, son of Agenor, was sent to find his sister Europa after her abduction. He founded the city of Thebes, whose citadel was named Cadmeia after him.

myths.name: Theban Saga
myths.summary: The saga of Thebes, centered on the cursed family of Labdacus, including Oedipus and Antigone, as treated by Sophocles.

myths.name: Abduction of Europa
myths.summary: Zeus, disguised as a bull, abducted Europa from Phoenicia and took her to Crete, where she became mother of Minos.

myths.name: Abduction of Chrysippus
myths.summary: Laius abducted Chrysippus, son of Pelops, in a chariot, as depicted on an Apulian bell-krater.

myths.name: Amphion and Zethus
myths.summary: Antiope gives birth to twin sons Amphion and Zethus, who are left to die but found by a shepherd. They later recognize their mother, avenge her by killing Lycus and Dirce, and become rulers of Cadmeia. Amphion builds the city walls with his lyre's music, and the city is renamed Thebes after Zethus' wife.

myths.name: Oedipus and the Sphinx
myths.summary: Oedipus, after unknowingly killing his father Laius, comes to Thebes and solves the riddle of the Sphinx, freeing the city. He becomes king and marries his mother Jocasta, fulfilling the prophecy.

myths.name: The Recognition of Oedipus
myths.summary: Years later, a plague afflicts Thebes. Oedipus discovers the truth about his parentage and crimes: he killed his father and married his mother. Jocasta hangs herself, and Oedipus blinds himself. Creon becomes regent, and Oedipus is banished.

myths.name: Oedipus at Colonus
myths.summary: Oedipus, after years of wandering, arrives at Colonus with Antigone. He is protected by Theseus and the Eumenides, defends his innocence, curses his son Polynices, and dies a miraculous death, becoming a hero.

myths.name: Oedipus Tyrannus
myths.summary: Oedipus unknowingly kills his father and marries his mother, fulfilling Apollo's prophecy. He discovers the truth and blinds himself.

myths.name: Antigone
myths.summary: Antigone defies Creon's decree to bury her brother Polynices, upholding unwritten laws, and dies as a result.

myths.name: Death of Oedipus
myths.summary: Oedipus, guided by Theseus, goes to a sacred grove at Colonus where he prepares for death. After washing and being called by a god, he sends his daughters away and only Theseus witnesses his miraculous disappearance. Oedipus becomes a hero bringing good to Attica.

myths.name: Seven against Thebes
myths.summary: After Oedipus' death, his sons Eteocles and Polynices quarrel over the throne. Polynices goes to Argos, marries the daughter of King Adrastus, and leads an army of seven champions to attack Thebes. The expedition fails; all leaders except Adrastus are killed. The war includes episodes at Nemea and the ambush of Tydeus.

myths.name: Epigoni
myths.summary: The sons of the Seven against Thebes, led by Alcmaeon, successfully attack Thebes ten years later and destroy the city.

myths.name: Tiresias
myths.summary: Tiresias, a blind prophet, was blinded by Athena for seeing her bathe, but given prophecy; he also judged a quarrel between Zeus and Hera about pleasure, leading to his blindness and gift of prophecy.

myths.name: Heracles
myths.summary: The infant Heracles strangles snakes sent by Hera; Tiresias interprets the miracle and foretells his labors.

myths.name: Tantalus and Pelops
myths.summary: Tantalus, favored by the gods, abused his privilege by serving his son Pelops as a feast to the gods. The gods recognized the deception and restored Pelops to life, replacing his shoulder with ivory. Tantalus was punished in the Underworld with eternal hunger and thirst.

myths.name: The Race of Pelops and Oenomaüs
myths.summary: Pelops sought to marry Hippodamia, daughter of King Oenomaüs, who challenged suitors to a chariot race. With help from Poseidon (who gave him a golden chariot) or by bribing Myrtilus to sabotage Oenomaüs' chariot, Pelops won the race and married Hippodamia.

myths.name: The Curse of Myrtilus
myths.summary: After winning the race, Pelops killed Myrtilus by throwing him into the sea when Myrtilus attempted to violate Hippodamia. As he died, Myrtilus cursed Pelops and his descendants, leading to the misfortunes of the House of Atreus.

myths.name: The Quarrel of Atreus and Thyestes
myths.summary: Atreus and Thyestes, sons of Pelops, quarreled over the kingdom of Mycenae. Thyestes seduced Atreus' wife Aërope and stole the golden-fleeced ram, but Zeus reversed the sun's course in anger. Atreus later pretended reconciliation and served Thyestes his own sons at a banquet.

myths.name: The Banquet of Thyestes
myths.summary: Atreus, to avenge his wife's adultery, killed Thyestes' sons and served them to Thyestes at a feast. Thyestes realized the truth too late and cursed Atreus as the sun hid from the crime.

myths.name: The Sacrifice of Iphigenia
myths.summary: Agamemnon sacrificed his daughter Iphigenia to appease Artemis and obtain favorable winds for the Trojan expedition. This act earned the hatred of his wife Clytemnestra.

myths.name: The Murder of Agamemnon
myths.summary: Upon returning from Troy with Cassandra, Agamemnon was murdered by his wife Clytemnestra and her lover Aegisthus. Clytemnestra justified the deed as vengeance for Iphigenia, while Aegisthus saw it as vengeance for Thyestes.

myths.name: Death of Agamemnon
myths.summary: Agamemnon returns from Troy and is murdered by his wife Clytemnestra and her lover Aegisthus. Clytemnestra traps him in a robe while he is bathing and stabs him, as described by Aeschylus.

myths.name: Iphigenia in Tauris
myths.summary: Orestes and Pylades travel to Tauris to fetch a statue of Artemis. They are captured and brought to the priestess Iphigenia, who recognizes Orestes. They deceive King Thoas and escape with the statue, returning to Greece.

myths.name: Andromache
myths.summary: Set in Phthia, Andromache, slave of Neoptolemus, has borne him a son, while his wife Hermione is childless. Hermione and Menelaüs plot to kill Andromache, but the action is interrupted by Neoptolemus' death at Delphi.

myths.name: Orestes
myths.summary: Euripides' play set after Clytemnestra's murder. Orestes and Electra are judged by Argives, plot to kill Helen and Hermione, but Apollo intervenes, making Helen immortal and arranging marriages: Orestes to Hermione, Pylades to Electra.

myths.name: Libation Bearers
myths.summary: Aeschylus' play about Orestes' return to Argos, reunion with Electra, and murder of Clytemnestra and Aegisthus to avenge Agamemnon. Orestes is motivated by Apollo's oracle and fear of Furies.

myths.name: Electra (Sophocles)
myths.summary: Sophocles' version of the Electra story, focusing on Electra's grief and hatred, her confrontation with Clytemnestra, and Orestes' return and vengeance.

myths.name: Orestes and the Three Electras
myths.summary: The story of Orestes' return to Argos to avenge his father Agamemnon's murder by killing his mother Clytemnestra and her lover Aegisthus, with focus on the character of Electra in Sophocles' version. The chapter includes the recognition scene, the false news of Orestes' death, and the final revenge.

myths.name: Electra (Euripides)
myths.summary: Euripides' version of the Electra myth: Orestes returns with Pylades, is recognized by Electra via a scar, and with Electra's help kills Aegisthus and then Clytemnestra. The play emphasizes psychological conflict and Electra's active role in the murder.

myths.name: Electra
myths.summary: Euripides' version of the matricide, focusing on Electra's role in urging Orestes to kill their mother Clytemnestra, and the aftermath with the Dioscuri's intervention.

myths.name: Birth of the Dioscuri and Helen
myths.summary: Leda, wife of Tyndareus, bore four children to Zeus who visited her as a swan: from two eggs came Polydeuces and Helen, and Castor and Clytemnestra.

myths.name: Quarrel of the Dioscuri with Idas and Lynceus
myths.summary: The Dioscuri quarreled with Idas and Lynceus over cattle division. Lynceus killed Castor, and Idas was destroyed by Zeus' thunderbolt. Polydeuces chose to share immortality with Castor, spending alternate days on Olympus and in Hades.

myths.name: Dioscuri as saviors of sailors
myths.summary: Castor and Polydeuces appear as St. Elmo's fire to calm storms and save sailors, as described in Homeric Hymn 33.

myths.name: The Judgment of Paris
myths.summary: At the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, Eris threw a golden apple 'For the most beautiful.' Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite claimed it. Zeus sent them to Paris, who chose Aphrodite after she promised him Helen, leading to the Trojan War.

myths.name: Stesichorus' Palinode
myths.summary: Stesichorus claimed that Helen never went to Troy but was detained in Egypt by King Proteus; a phantom went to Troy instead.

myths.name: Wedding of Peleus and Thetis
myths.summary: The Olympian gods attended the wedding; Eris, not invited, threw the golden apple that sparked the Judgment of Paris.

myths.name: Judgment of Paris
myths.summary: Paris, a Trojan prince, is chosen to judge which goddess—Hera, Athena, or Aphrodite—is the fairest. Aphrodite promises him Helen of Sparta, and he awards her the golden apple, leading to the Trojan War.

myths.name: Achilles' Disguise at Scyros
myths.summary: Thetis disguised Achilles as a girl among the daughters of Lycomedes to prevent him from going to Troy. Odysseus and Diomedes exposed him by offering weapons and sounding a trumpet, revealing his true nature.

myths.name: Sacrifice of Iphigenia
myths.summary: Agamemnon sacrificed his daughter Iphigenia at Aulis to appease Artemis and allow the Greek fleet to sail. In some versions, Artemis saved her and substituted a stag.

myths.name: Calchas' Prophecy
myths.summary: Calchas interpreted an omen of a snake devouring eight chicks and their mother, then turning to stone, to mean the Greeks would fight for nine years before capturing Troy in the tenth.

myths.name: Philoctetes on Lemnos
myths.summary: Philoctetes was bitten by a snake and abandoned on Lemnos due to his wound's stench. Later, Odysseus and Diomedes fetched him after Helenus prophesied that Heracles' bow and arrows were needed to capture Troy.

myths.name: Achilles Heals Telephus
myths.summary: Achilles wounded Telephus, son of Heracles, in Mysia. Later, Telephus was healed by Achilles, possibly with rust from the spear.

myths.name: Telephus
myths.summary: Telephus, wounded by Achilles' spear, was told by the Delphic oracle that 'he that wounded shall heal.' He went to the Greek army disguised as a beggar, and scrapings from Achilles' spear healed him.

myths.name: Protesilaüs and Laodamia
myths.summary: Protesilaüs, the first Greek to leap ashore at Troy, was killed by Hector. His wife Laodamia grieved so much that Hermes brought him back from Hades for a few hours; when he was taken again, she killed herself.

myths.name: The Iliad
myths.summary: The Iliad covers events from the quarrel between Achilles and Agamemnon to the ransoming and burial of Hector. Agamemnon takes Briseïs from Achilles, causing Achilles to withdraw from battle. The Greeks suffer, and the Trojans gain success. Key episodes include the duel between Menelaüs and Paris, and Hector's farewell to Andromache.

myths.name: Quarrel of Achilles and Agamemnon
myths.summary: Achilles and Agamemnon quarrel over Briseïs, leading Achilles to withdraw from battle.

myths.name: Death of Patroclus
myths.summary: Patroclus is killed by Hector while wearing Achilles' armor.

myths.name: Armor of Achilles
myths.summary: Thetis obtains new armor from Hephaestus for Achilles, including the famous shield.

myths.name: Return of Achilles to Battle
myths.summary: Achilles ends his quarrel, receives Briseïs and new armor, and returns to fight Hector.

myths.name: Achilles fights Scamander
myths.summary: Achilles fights the river-god Scamander, filling the river with Trojan corpses.

myths.name: Death of Hector
myths.summary: Achilles kills Hector after chasing him around Troy, with Athena's help.

myths.name: Funeral of Patroclus
myths.summary: Achilles holds funeral games and sacrifices Trojan prisoners on Patroclus' pyre.

myths.name: Ransom of Hector
myths.summary: Priam ransoms Hector's body from Achilles, leading to a moment of compassion.

myths.name: Funeral of Hector
myths.summary: The Trojans mourn Hector for nine days; Andromache, Hecuba, and Helen lament.

myths.name: Embassy to Achilles
myths.summary: Odysseus and others try to persuade Achilles to return to battle.

myths.name: Theomachy
myths.summary: Gods fight each other on the battlefield in two episodes (Iliad Books 5 and 20-21), highlighting the gap between mortal and divine.

myths.name: Wounding of Aphrodite
myths.summary: Diomedes wounds Aphrodite in battle; she returns to Olympus and is comforted by her mother Dione.

myths.name: Wounding of Ares
myths.summary: Diomedes wounds Ares, who complains to Zeus but finds little sympathy.

myths.name: Funeral Games of Patroclus
myths.summary: Achilles presides over funeral games for Patroclus, showing princely dignity and making peace between competitors.

myths.name: Achilles and Penthesilea
myths.summary: Achilles kills the Amazon queen Penthesilea; in some versions he falls in love with her at the moment of death. He then kills Thersites for taunting him and is purified by Odysseus.

myths.name: Achilles and Memnon
myths.summary: Achilles kills Memnon, son of Eos and Tithonus, leader of the Ethiopians. Memnon's followers are turned into birds.

myths.name: Death of Achilles
myths.summary: Achilles is fatally wounded in the heel by an arrow shot by Paris with Apollo's help. His corpse is recovered by Ajax and buried at Sigeum.

myths.name: Funeral of Achilles
myths.summary: Thetis and the Muses mourn Achilles; his bones are mixed with Patroclus' in a golden urn; Thetis gives funeral games.

myths.name: Sacrifice of Polyxena
myths.summary: Achilles' ghost demands the sacrifice of Polyxena at his tomb; Euripides' Hecuba dramatizes this.

myths.name: Odysseus and Ajax Compete for Armor
myths.summary: Odysseus and Ajax compete for Achilles' armor after his death, each making a speech.

myths.name: Judgment of the Arms of Achilles
myths.summary: After Achilles' death, his armor was awarded to Odysseus over Ajax. Ajax went mad, slaughtered sheep, and killed himself. From his blood sprang a flower with his initials.

myths.name: Death of Ajax
myths.summary: Ajax, maddened by losing the armor, killed himself by falling on his sword. From his blood sprang a flower with the letters AI-AI.

myths.name: The Wooden Horse
myths.summary: The Greeks built a hollow wooden horse, hid warriors inside, and left it outside Troy. The Trojans brought it inside despite warnings, and at night the Greeks emerged to sack the city.

myths.name: Fall of Troy
myths.summary: The Greeks sack Troy with the help of hostile gods. Aeneas escapes with his father Anchises, son Ascanius, and the household gods, but his wife Creusa is lost. Venus reveals to Aeneas the divine forces destroying the city.

myths.name: Calydonian Boar Hunt
myths.summary: King Oeneus offends Artemis, who sends a giant boar to ravage Calydon. Meleager gathers heroes including Atalanta to hunt it. Atalanta first wounds the boar, Meleager kills it and gives the skin to her. Meleager kills his uncles in a quarrel, causing his mother Althaea to burn a magical log that ends his life.

myths.name: Returns of the Greek Leaders
myths.summary: The returns of Greek leaders from Troy, including Agamemnon, Menelaüs, Nestor, Diomedes, Idomeneus, Philoctetes, and Neoptolemus, with various fates: some murdered, some exiled, some founding colonies in Italy. The story of Ajax's death and Nauplius' revenge is included.

myths.name: Nekuia
myths.summary: Odysseus' visit to the Underworld to consult the prophet Tiresias; he performs a ritual sacrifice and speaks with ghosts of the dead.

myths.name: The Bow and the Killing of the Suitors
myths.summary: Odysseus, disguised as a beggar, strings his bow effortlessly and shoots an arrow through twelve axes, then kills the leading suitor Antinoüs and, with Telemachus and servants, slaughters all the suitors. The disloyal servants are hanged, and the goatherd Melanthius is mutilated and killed.

myths.name: The Returns and the Odyssey
myths.summary: The overall narrative of Odysseus' return to Ithaca after the Trojan War, including his encounters with various characters and his eventual reunion with Penelope. The chapter also covers Telemachus' journey to Pylos and Sparta, and the background of Odysseus' parentage.

myths.name: The Test of the Bow
myths.summary: Penelope devises a contest where the suitors must string Odysseus' bow and shoot an arrow through twelve axes. Odysseus, disguised as a beggar, succeeds and then slaughters the suitors.

myths.name: The Slaughter of the Suitors
myths.summary: After stringing the bow, Odysseus, with the help of Telemachus and Athena, kills all the suitors in the hall and cleanses the palace.

myths.name: The Recognition of Odysseus
myths.summary: Penelope tests Odysseus by asking Euryclea to move their bed, revealing the secret of its construction. Odysseus reacts angrily, proving his identity, and they are reunited.

myths.name: Naming Odysseus
myths.summary: Autolycus names the infant Odysseus, meaning 'man of pain' or 'hateful', reflecting his future sufferings and causing pain to others.

myths.name: Odysseus and Athena
myths.summary: Athena, disguised as a shepherd, meets Odysseus on Ithaca after his return. They recognize each other's cunning and plan his revenge against the suitors.

myths.name: The End of Odysseus' Life
myths.summary: Tiresias prophesies that after killing the suitors, Odysseus must travel inland with an oar until he finds people who know nothing of the sea, then make a sacrifice to Poseidon.

myths.name: Telegonia
myths.summary: Lost epic continuing Odysseus's story after the Odyssey; Telegonus, son of Odysseus and Circe, travels to Ithaca, kills Odysseus unknowingly, and later marries Penelope; Circe marries Telemachus.

myths.name: Aeolus
myths.summary: Story of Macareus and Canace, children of Aeolus, who fell in love and had a child; Aeolus forced them to suicide.

myths.name: Contest of Poseidon and Hera
myths.summary: Phoroneus decided in favor of Hera in the contest for the land between Poseidon and Hera. In anger, Poseidon dried up the Argive rivers.

myths.name: Perseus and the Gorgon
myths.summary: Perseus, son of Zeus and Danaë, is sent by King Polydectes to fetch the head of Medusa. With help from Hermes and Athena, he obtains magic objects from nymphs, forces the Graeae to reveal their location, and beheads Medusa using a reflective shield. He uses the head to turn Polydectes to stone.

myths.name: Andromeda
myths.summary: Andromeda, daughter of Cepheus and Cassiepea, is offered as a sacrifice to a sea-monster sent by Poseidon because Cassiepea boasted she was more beautiful than the Nereids. Perseus rescues her and later marries her.

myths.name: Perseus and the Gorgon Medusa
myths.summary: Perseus, son of Danaë and Zeus, is sent by Polydectes to fetch the head of Medusa. With help from Hermes and Athena, he obtains winged sandals, a cap of invisibility, a kibisis, and a scimitar. He beheads Medusa, and from her body springs Pegasus.

myths.name: Perseus and Andromeda
myths.summary: Cepheus and Cassiopeia's boasting angers Poseidon, who sends a sea-monster. Andromeda is chained to a rock as sacrifice. Perseus kills the monster, marries Andromeda, and turns Phineus to stone with Medusa's head. Their son Perses is left as heir.

myths.name: The Origin of Libyan Snakes, the Atlas Range, and Coral
myths.summary: As Perseus flies over Libya, Medusa's blood drips and creates poisonous snakes. Atlas is turned to stone and becomes a mountain range. Coral is created when Perseus places Medusa's head on seaweed, which hardens.

myths.name: Polydectes and Perseus' Return to Argos
myths.summary: Perseus returns to Seriphos, finds Danaë and Dictys at an altar. He turns Polydectes and his followers to stone, makes Dictys king, and returns magic objects to the gods.

myths.name: The Death of Acrisius
myths.summary: Acrisius flees to Larissa to avoid Perseus. Perseus accidentally kills him with a discus at athletic games. Perseus then exchanges kingdoms with Megapenthes and becomes king of Tiryns, founding Mycenae.

myths.name: The Family of Inachus
myths.summary: Io, daughter of Inachus, is beloved by Zeus, turned into a cow by Hera, guarded by Argus, and rescued by Hermes. She wanders to Egypt, where she gives birth to Epaphus and is identified with Isis.

myths.name: The Descendants of Io
myths.summary: Epaphus founds cities in Egypt. His daughter Libya gives name to North Africa. His twin sons Agenor and Belus become ancestors of Cadmus, Europa, Minos, Aegyptus, and Danaüs.

myths.name: The Daughters of Danaüs
myths.summary: Danaüs and his fifty daughters flee to Argos. The fifty sons of Aegyptus pursue and marry them. Danaüs orders his daughters to kill their husbands; all obey except Hypermnestra, who spares Lynceus. The Danaïds are punished in the Underworld.

myths.name: Amymone and the Spring
myths.summary: Amymone, a Danaïd, was sent to find water. A satyr attempted to seduce her, but Poseidon saved her and lay with her, causing a spring to burst from a rock with his trident.

myths.name: Bellerophon and the Chimera
myths.summary: Bellerophon, grandson of Sisyphus, was sent by King Iobates to kill the Chimera, a fire-breathing monster. He succeeded with the help of Pegasus, then fought the Solymi and the Amazons, and later killed all ambushers sent by Iobates. He married Iobates' daughter and received half the kingdom.

myths.name: Bellerophon and Pegasus
myths.summary: Poseidon gave the winged horse Pegasus to Bellerophon, but he could not master it until Athena gave him a magic bridle in a dream. He then harnessed Pegasus and performed his labors.

myths.name: Bellerophon's Fall
myths.summary: Bellerophon attempted to ride Pegasus to heaven to join the gods, but Pegasus threw him off, and he wandered alone in sorrow, hated by the gods.

myths.name: Stheneboea
myths.summary: In Euripides' tragedy, Bellerophon returned to Tiryns after his labors and killed Stheneboea by luring her onto Pegasus and throwing her into the sea.

myths.name: Birth of Heracles
myths.summary: Zeus, disguised as Amphitryon, lay with Alcmena, who conceived Heracles. Hera, hostile, delayed his birth and sent snakes to kill him, but the infant Heracles strangled them. Tiresias foretold his future labors and apotheosis.

myths.name: Early Exploits
myths.summary: Heracles was educated by various teachers, killed Linus with a lyre, and was sent to Mt. Cithaeron. There he killed a lion, entertained by Thespius, and freed Thebes from the Minyans, receiving Megara as wife.

myths.name: Madness of Heracles
myths.summary: Hera caused Heracles to go mad, killing his wife Megara and their children. After recovering, he sought purification and was told by the Delphic oracle to serve Eurystheus for twelve years, performing labors to gain immortality.

myths.name: Twelve Labors
myths.summary: Heracles performed twelve labors for Eurystheus: Nemean Lion, Lernaean Hydra, Cerynean Hind, Erymanthian Boar, Augean Stables, Stymphalian Birds, Cretan Bull, Mares of Diomedes, Girdle of Hippolyta, Cattle of Geryon, Apples of the Hesperides, and Cerberus. The first six were in the Peloponnese, the last six elsewhere.

myths.name: The Twelve Labors
myths.summary: Heracles performed twelve labors for King Eurystheus, including the Nemean Lion, Lernaean Hydra, Stymphalian Birds, Cretan Bull, Mares of Diomedes, Girdle of Hippolyta, Cattle of Geryon, Apples of the Hesperides, Cerberus, and Augean Stables. The labors are depicted on the metopes of the Temple of Zeus at Olympia.

myths.name: The Cretan Bull
myths.summary: Heracles caught the Cretan Bull that Minos had refused to sacrifice to Poseidon and brought it to Eurystheus. The bull was later released and eventually caught by Theseus at Marathon.

myths.name: The Mares of Diomedes
myths.summary: Heracles captured the man-eating mares of Diomedes, son of Ares, and tamed them by feeding them Diomedes himself. He then took them to Argos. On the way, he restored Alcestis to her husband Admetus by wrestling Thanatos.

myths.name: The Girdle of Hippolyta
myths.summary: Heracles was sent to fetch the magical girdle of Hippolyta, queen of the Amazons. He killed her in battle and took the girdle. On his return, he rescued Hesione from a sea-monster at Troy and later sacked Troy after being cheated by Laomedon.

myths.name: The Cattle of Geryon
myths.summary: Heracles traveled to the island of Erythia to fetch the cattle of the three-bodied monster Geryon. He killed Geryon, his herdsman Eurytion, and the two-headed dog Orthus, and sailed back in Helius' golden cup. He set up the Pillars of Heracles at the Straits of Gibraltar. On his return, he had various adventures including killing Cacus, Eryx, and Alcyoneus. Herodotus tells a version where Heracles fathered Scythes with Echidna.

myths.name: Melampus and the Cattle of Phylacus
myths.summary: Melampus helped his brother Bias obtain the cattle of Phylacus as a bride-price for Pero. He was imprisoned but learned from woodworms that the roof would collapse. After being moved, he cured Iphiclus' impotence by finding a knife rust, and received the cattle as reward.

myths.name: Apples of the Hesperides
myths.summary: Heracles was tasked with fetching the golden apples from the garden of the Hesperides. He learned the location from Nereus after wrestling him, then either killed Ladon or enlisted Atlas's help to obtain the apples. He also killed Busiris and Antaeus on the journey, and freed Prometheus.

myths.name: Cerberus
myths.summary: Heracles' final labor was to capture Cerberus, the three-headed hound of Hades. With help from Hermes and Athena, he wrestled Cerberus in the underworld, brought him to Eurystheus, and then returned him. In Hades, he freed Theseus and saw the ghost of Meleager, who prompted him to marry Deianira.

myths.name: Cycnus
myths.summary: Heracles, with Iolaus as charioteer and aided by Athena, killed Cycnus, son of Ares, who robbed travelers in Thessaly. He also wounded Ares.

myths.name: Syleus
myths.summary: Heracles destroyed the vineyard of Syleus, who forced passers-by to work, and then killed Syleus.

myths.name: Cercopes
myths.summary: Heracles caught the dwarf tricksters Cercopes, but released them after they made him laugh by joking about his sunburned backside.

myths.name: Hylas
myths.summary: While on the Argo, Heracles' beloved Hylas was pulled into a spring by water-nymphs. Heracles searched for him so long that the Argonauts sailed away without him.

myths.name: Neleus
myths.summary: Heracles attacked Neleus, king of Pylos, for refusing to purify him after the murder of Iphitus. He killed eleven of Neleus' sons, including Periclymenus, but spared Nestor. During this expedition, he wounded Hades and Hera.

myths.name: Deianira and Nessus
myths.summary: Heracles married Deianira after wrestling the river-god Achelous. On their journey, the centaur Nessus attempted to violate Deianira, and Heracles shot him. Dying, Nessus gave Deianira his blood as a love charm.

myths.name: Iole
myths.summary: Heracles fell in love with Iole, but her father Eurytus refused to give her to him. Later, Heracles killed Iole's brother Iphitus by throwing him from a citadel.

myths.name: Death of Heracles
myths.summary: Deïanira, jealous of Iole, sends Heracles a robe dipped in the blood of Nessus. The poison burns Heracles, who in agony kills Lichas and has himself carried to a pyre on Mt. Oeta. He gives his bow to Poeas, instructs Hyllus to marry Iole, and ascends to Olympus to marry Hebe.

myths.name: Heracles and Omphale
myths.summary: After killing Iphitus, Heracles is purified but must be sold as a slave. He serves Omphale, queen of Lydia, for a year, performing women's work.

myths.name: Heracles and the Tripod
myths.summary: When the Pythia refuses to answer Heracles, he tries to steal the sacred tripod to establish his own oracle. Apollo wrestles him, and Zeus intervenes with a thunderbolt.

myths.name: Choice of Heracles
myths.summary: Prodicus tells a parable where young Heracles chooses between Pleasure and Virtue, opting for the latter.

myths.name: Heraclidae
myths.summary: After Heracles' death, his mother Alcmena and his children were persecuted by Eurystheus. They fled to Athens, where Demophon received them. Macaria sacrificed herself, and Iolaüs captured Eurystheus. In some versions, Alcmena married Rhadamanthys or was transported to the Elysian Fields.

myths.name: Return of the Heraclidae
myths.summary: The descendants of Heracles, led by Hyllus and later Temenus, attempted to reclaim the Peloponnese. After a truce of one hundred years, they succeeded with the help of Oxylus, dividing the land into Sparta, Argos, and Messene. The story explains the Dorian invasion of Greece.

myths.name: Labors of Heracles
myths.summary: Heracles performed twelve labors for Eurystheus, including slaying the Nemean lion, capturing the Cerynitian hind, and taking the cattle of Geryon. The labors are referenced throughout the chapter.

myths.name: Contest of Poseidon and Athena for Attica
myths.summary: Poseidon and Athena competed for possession of Attica. Poseidon struck the Acropolis with his trident producing a salt spring, while Athena produced an olive tree. Athena won and became the patron of Athens.

myths.name: Birth of Erichthonius
myths.summary: Hephaestus attempted to violate Athena; his semen fell on the ground and from it sprang Erichthonius, who was partly serpent-shaped. Athena entrusted him to the daughters of Cecrops in a chest.

myths.name: Daughters of Cecrops
myths.summary: Athena gave the chest containing Erichthonius to the daughters of Cecrops, forbidding them to look inside. They disobeyed, saw either snakes or Erichthonius with snakelike body, and driven mad, hurled themselves off the Acropolis.

myths.name: Herse and Hermes
myths.summary: Hermes loved Herse. Aglauros asked for gold to help him, but Athena filled her with envy. Aglauros tried to prevent Hermes from entering Herse's chamber, and Hermes turned her into a rock. Hermes then lay with Herse, and their son was Cephalus.

myths.name: Cephalus and Procris
myths.summary: Cephalus was tempted by Aurora to test Procris' faithfulness. In disguise he attempted to seduce her, and when she nearly yielded, he revealed himself. Procris fled and joined Artemis, who gave her a hound and javelin. Later reconciled, Procris returned. Cephalus, calling for the breeze (Aura), was overheard and misreported as calling a nymph. Procris spied on him, and he accidentally killed her with the javelin.

myths.name: War with Eleusis
myths.summary: Erechtheus defended Athens against the Eleusinians led by Eumolpus, son of Poseidon. With approval of his wife Praxithea, he sacrificed one or all three of his daughters to secure victory. He killed Eumolpus, and Poseidon killed Erechtheus with his trident.

myths.name: Sacrifice of Erechtheus' daughters
myths.summary: Erechtheus sacrificed his daughters to ensure victory against the Eleusinians. In Euripides' Ion, Creusa says all her sisters were sacrificed except herself, who was a baby.

myths.name: Philomela, Procne, and Tereus
myths.summary: Tereus married Procne and later violated her sister Philomela, cutting out her tongue and imprisoning her. Philomela wove the story into a tapestry and sent it to Procne. The myth is told by Ovid.

myths.name: The Rape of Philomela
myths.summary: Tereus rapes Philomela, cuts out her tongue, and imprisons her. Philomela weaves the story into a tapestry and sends it to her sister Procne. Procne, in revenge, kills her son Itys and serves him to Tereus. The sisters are transformed into birds, and Tereus into a hoopoe.

myths.name: Ion
myths.summary: Creusa, daughter of Erechtheus, is loved by Apollo and bears Ion, whom she exposes. Ion is saved by Hermes and raised at Delphi. Years later, Creusa and her husband Xuthus consult the oracle; Xuthus is told to greet the first person he meets as his son, who is Ion. Creusa, not recognizing him, tries to kill him, but Athena intervenes and mother and son are reunited. Ion becomes ancestor of the Ionic tribes.

myths.name: Orithyia and Boreas
myths.summary: Boreas, the North Wind, carries off Orithyia, daughter of Erechtheus, to Thrace. She becomes mother of Zetes, Calaïs, Cleopatra, and Chione. Cleopatra marries Phineus; Chione bears Eumolpus to Poseidon.

myths.name: The Early Kings of Athens
myths.summary: Erechtheus is succeeded by Cecrops, then Pandion. Pandion is driven out by Metion, flees to Megara, and fathers Aegeus, Pallas, Nisus, and Lycus. After Pandion's death, the brothers recover Athens; Aegeus becomes sovereign.

myths.name: Theseus' Six Labors
myths.summary: On his journey from Troezen to Athens, Theseus performs six deeds: kills Periphetes at Epidaurus, kills Sinis at the Isthmus, kills the Crommyonian sow, kills Sciron at the Cliffs of Sciron, kills Cercyon at Eleusis, and kills Procrustes near Athens.

myths.name: Theseus Recognized by Aegeus
myths.summary: Theseus arrives in Athens. Medea, Aegeus' wife, tries to poison him, but Aegeus recognizes Theseus by his sword and stops the poisoning. Theseus is publicly recognized as son and successor. Later, Theseus kills Pallas and his sons to secure his position.

myths.name: Bull of Marathon
myths.summary: Theseus captures the bull of Marathon (previously brought from Crete by Heracles) and sacrifices it to Apollo Delphinius. On the way, he is entertained by Hecale, who dies before his return; Theseus orders that she be honored at a festival to Zeus Hecalus.

myths.name: Ariadne on Naxos
myths.summary: Theseus deserts Ariadne on the island of Naxos (Dia). Dionysus finds her, marries her, and places her wreath in the sky as the constellation Corona. Various versions exist: Homer says Artemis killed Ariadne; another says she died in childbirth; she was later honored as Ariadne Aphrodite.

myths.name: Theseus Becomes King of Athens
myths.summary: Theseus forgets to change the black sail to white, causing Aegeus to think he is dead and throw himself into the sea (named Aegean). Theseus becomes king and is credited with uniting Attica (synoecism) and refounding the Isthmian Games.

myths.name: The Amazons
myths.summary: Theseus joins Heracles in an expedition against the Amazons and receives Antiope as his share, who bears him Hippolytus. The Amazons invade Attica in revenge but are defeated by Theseus; Antiope dies in the battle.

myths.name: Theseus and Pirithoüs
myths.summary: Theseus and Pirithoüs, king of the Lapiths, are friends. Theseus helps fight the centaurs at Pirithoüs' wedding. They vow to help each other get wives: Theseus kidnaps Helen (then a child), and Pirithoüs attempts to abduct Persephone. While they are in the Underworld, the Dioscuri recover Helen. Pirithoüs is trapped in Hades; Theseus is freed by Heracles.

myths.name: Theseus, Phaedra, and Hippolytus
myths.summary: Theseus marries Phaedra, who falls in love with her stepson Hippolytus. When her nurse reveals the secret to Hippolytus, Phaedra hangs herself and leaves a letter falsely accusing Hippolytus of seduction. Theseus banishes Hippolytus and calls on Poseidon to destroy him.

myths.name: Theseus as Champion of the Oppressed
myths.summary: Theseus gave refuge to exiled Oedipus and, in Euripides' Suppliant Women, championed the mothers of the Seven against Thebes. He attacked Thebes and brought back the bodies of the dead Argive leaders for burial. Evadne, widow of Capaneus, threw herself into his pyre.

myths.name: Other Adventures of Theseus
myths.summary: Theseus was said to have been an Argonaut and participated in the Calydonian boar hunt. He was driven out of Athens by Menestheus and killed on Scyros by Lycomedes. Later, Cimon brought his bones back to Athens.

myths.name: Demophon
myths.summary: Demophon, son of Theseus, loved the Thracian princess Phyllis. He left her, swearing to return, but never did. She hanged herself and became an almond tree. When he returned and embraced the tree, it burst into leaf.

myths.name: Codrus
myths.summary: Codrus, the last king of Athens, sacrificed himself for his city. An oracle said the side whose king was killed would win. Codrus disguised himself, provoked enemy soldiers, and was killed, leading to Athenian victory.

myths.name: Minos and Daedalus
myths.summary: Minos prayed to Poseidon for a bull but kept it, so Poseidon made Pasiphaë fall in love with the bull. Daedalus built a hollow cow for her to mate with the bull, resulting in the Minotaur, kept in the Labyrinth. Daedalus later fled Crete with his son Icarus.

myths.name: The Flight of Icarus
myths.summary: Daedalus made wings of feathers and wax to escape Crete with his son Icarus. Icarus ignored his father's warning not to fly too close to the sun; the wax melted, and he fell into the sea, which was named the Icarian Sea.

myths.name: Daedalus in Sicily
myths.summary: Daedalus fled to Sicily and was received by King Cocalus. Minos pursued him and discovered his location by using a spiral shell that only Daedalus could thread. Minos was then killed by Cocalus' daughters in boiling water.

myths.name: Minos and the Spiral Shell
myths.summary: Minos used a spiral shell as a ruse to find Daedalus in Sicily. He asked Cocalus to have it threaded, and when Cocalus returned it threaded, Minos knew Daedalus was there.

myths.name: Catreus and Althaemenes
myths.summary: An oracle foretold that Althaemenes would kill his father Catreus. Althaemenes fled to Rhodes with his sister Apemosyne to avoid this fate. Apemosyne was seduced by Hermes and killed by Althaemenes. Later, Catreus came to Rhodes and was killed by Althaemenes in a skirmish, fulfilling the oracle. Althaemenes was honored as a hero by the Rhodians.

myths.name: Glaucus and Polyidus
myths.summary: Glaucus, son of Minos, drowned in a vat of honey. Minos consulted an oracle, which said that the person who could find a simile for a magic calf would find and restore Glaucus. The seer Polyidus likened the calf to a mulberry, found Glaucus' corpse, and later restored him to life using an herb observed from snakes. Minos then forced Polyidus to teach Glaucus the seer's art, but Glaucus forgot it when Polyidus told him to spit into his mouth.

myths.name: Scylla and Nisus
myths.summary: Nisus, king of Megara, had a purple lock of hair that protected the city. His daughter Scylla fell in love with Minos and cut off the lock to betray the city. Minos rejected her, and she was turned into a sea bird (ciris), while Nisus became a sea eagle pursuing her.

myths.name: Phrixus and Helle
myths.summary: Athamas' wife Ino plots to kill his children Phrixus and Helle. Their mother Nephele sends a golden-fleeced ram to rescue them. Helle falls off and drowns in the straits named Hellespont. Phrixus reaches Colchis, sacrifices the ram, and gives the fleece to King Aeëtes.

myths.name: Quest for the Golden Fleece
myths.summary: Jason, rightful heir to Iolcus, is sent by Pelias to retrieve the Golden Fleece from Colchis. He assembles a crew of heroes (the Argonauts) and sails on the Argo. After many adventures, he reaches Colchis and, with the help of Medea, performs tasks to obtain the fleece.

myths.name: Argonautica
myths.summary: The epic voyage of Jason and the Argonauts from Iolcus to Colchis and back, including adventures at Lemnos, Cyzicus, Cios, with Amycus, Phineus, and the Symplegades.

myths.name: Hypsipyle and the Lemnian Women
myths.summary: The Lemnian women, punished by Aphrodite, kill all men on the island except King Thoas, saved by his daughter Hypsipyle. The Argonauts arrive and stay for a year, fathering children. Hypsipyle later becomes a slave nurse of Opheltes.

myths.name: Cyzicus and Cios
myths.summary: The Argonauts are welcomed by King Cyzicus of the Doliones. After leaving, they are driven back by winds and in a night battle kill Cyzicus. Later at Cios, Hylas is lost and Heracles leaves the expedition.

myths.name: Amycus
myths.summary: The Argonauts encounter the Bebryces and their king Amycus, a son of Poseidon who forces strangers to box. Polydeuces fights and kills him.

myths.name: Phineus and the Harpies
myths.summary: The blind prophet Phineus is tormented by Harpies who steal his food. Zetes and Calaïs pursue them until Iris stops them. Phineus then advises the Argonauts about the Symplegades.

myths.name: Jason at Colchis
myths.summary: Aeëtes sets Jason impossible tasks: yoking fire-breathing bulls and plowing a field. With Medea's help, Jason succeeds and obtains the Golden Fleece.

myths.name: Return of the Argonauts
myths.summary: After obtaining the fleece, Jason and Medea flee Colchis, pursued by the Colchians led by Apsyrtus, whom Jason kills. Their journey takes them to Circe, past Scylla and Charybdis, to the Phaeacians where they marry, then to Libya where they carry the Argo across the desert, and finally to Crete where they defeat the bronze giant Talus.

myths.name: Jason and Medea in Greece
myths.summary: At Iolcus, Medea tricks Pelias' daughters into killing him by pretending to rejuvenate him. Jason and Medea are driven out by Acastus and go to Corinth, where Jason becomes king through marriage. Medea resists Zeus' advances and is rewarded by Hera with immortality for her children.

myths.name: Medea
myths.summary: Euripides' tragedy focusing on Medea's revenge against Jason after he divorces her to marry Glauce. She kills Glauce, Creon, and her own children, then escapes to Athens.

myths.name: Jason and Medea in Euripides
myths.summary: The play Medea by Euripides depicts the confrontation between Jason and Medea after Jason abandons Medea to marry the daughter of Creon, king of Corinth. Medea, feeling betrayed, plots revenge, ultimately killing Creon's daughter and her own children. The excerpt includes the agon between Jason and Medea, where they argue over past deeds and responsibilities.

myths.name: Medea's Revenge
myths.summary: Medea, betrayed by Jason who marries Creusa, feigns reconciliation and sends poisoned gifts to Creusa, killing her and her father Creon. She then kills her own children to spite Jason and escapes in a chariot given by Helius.

places.description: Village near which Theseus killed the monstrous sow.

places.name: Cliffs of Sciron
places.description: Location in the Megarid where Sciron operated.

places.name: Megara
places.description: City where Pandion fled and where Nisus became king.

places.name: Ionia
places.description: Region in Asia Minor colonized by descendants of Ion.

places.name: River Ilissus
places.description: River in Athens where Orithyia was playing when Boreas carried her off.

places.name: Labyrinth
places.description: Maze in Crete built to contain the Minotaur.

places.name: Aphidnae
places.description: Attic village where Helen was kept after her kidnapping.

places.name: Mare Icarium
places.description: Sea named after Icarus, where he fell.

places.name: Lebinthos
places.description: Island; on the right during Icarus' flight in Ovid's account.

places.name: Calymne
places.description: Island; on the right during Icarus' flight in Ovid's account.

places.name: Camicus
places.description: City in Sicily ruled by King Cocalus.

places.name: Euxine Sea
places.description: The Black Sea, where the main part of the Argonautic saga takes place.

places.name: Hellespont
places.description: Straits between Europe and Asia (Dardanelles), named after Helle who fell there.

places.name: Propontis
places.description: Sea of Marmara, where Cyzicus is located.

places.name: Cyzicus
places.description: City on the Propontis, home of the Doliones and King Cyzicus.

places.name: Cios
places.description: Port on the Asiatic shore of the Propontis where Hylas was lost.

places.name: Bebryces
places.description: Land of the Bebryces, a Bithynian tribe, where Amycus ruled.

places.name: Salmydessus
places.description: City on the Euxine shore of Thrace, home of King Phineus.

places.name: Strophades Islands
places.description: Islands where the Harpies were pursued and stopped by Iris.

places.name: Symplegades
places.description: Clashing Rocks at the western end of the Black Sea, which the Argo passed through.

places.name: Mariandyni
places.description: Land of the Mariandyni, whose king Lycus received the Argonauts.

places.name: Phasis River
places.description: River in Colchis up which the Argo sailed.

places.name: Danube
places.description: River near whose mouth Jason killed Apsyrtus.

places.name: Lake Tritonis
places.description: Lake in Libya where the Argonauts were guided by Triton.

places.name: Phaeacia
places.description: Land of the Phaeacians, where Jason and Medea married.

places.name: Syrtes
places.description: Shoals off Libya where the Argonauts were stranded.

places.name: Vani
places.description: Modern town in Georgia, corresponding to ancient Colchis.

concepts.name: myth
concepts.definition: From Greek mythos, meaning word, speech, tale, or story; a traditional story, often about gods and humans.

concepts.name: true myth
concepts.definition: Stories primarily concerned with the gods and humankind's relations with them.

concepts.name: saga
concepts.definition: Also called legend; stories with a perceptible relationship to history, rooted in historical fact.

concepts.name: legend
concepts.definition: Synonym for saga; stories with historical roots.

concepts.name: folktale
concepts.definition: Stories of adventure, often with fantastic beings, where the hero triumphs; primarily for entertainment.

concepts.name: fairytale
concepts.definition: Short, imaginative, traditional tales with high moral and magical content, often for the young.

concepts.name: etiology
concepts.definition: From Greek aitia (cause); theory that myth explains the origin of some fact or custom.

concepts.name: cosmogony
concepts.definition: Origin myth about the creation of the world.

concepts.name: Euhemerism
concepts.definition: Theory that gods were men deified for their great deeds.

concepts.name: Allegory
concepts.definition: Sustained metaphor where details of a story are symbols of universal truths.

concepts.name: Nature myths
concepts.definition: Theory by Max Müller that all myths refer to meteorological and cosmological phenomena.

concepts.name: Oedipus complex
concepts.definition: Freudian concept of a man's sexual impulses toward his mother and hatred toward his father.

concepts.name: Electra complex
concepts.definition: Jungian term for a daughter's love for her father and hostility toward her mother.

concepts.name: Dream-work
concepts.definition: Mental process consisting of condensation, displacement, and representation.

concepts.name: Collective unconscious
concepts.definition: Jungian concept of inherited psychic tendencies of the race, expressed in archetypes.

concepts.name: Archetype
concepts.definition: Jungian term for traditional expressions of collective dreams, inherited behavior patterns.

concepts.name: Anima
concepts.definition: Jungian archetype of the female that each man has within him.

concepts.name: Animus
concepts.definition: Jungian archetype of the male that a woman instinctively harbors within her.

concepts.name: Westermarck effect
concepts.definition: Theory that human avoidance of incest is genetic and epigenetic.

concepts.name: Structuralism
concepts.definition: A theoretical approach to mythology that analyzes myths into their component parts, often focusing on binary oppositions and underlying structures.

concepts.name: Ritualist theory
concepts.definition: The theory that myth implies ritual and ritual implies myth, closely connecting myth with religion and ritual.

concepts.name: Myth as Social Charters
concepts.definition: The theory that myths explain and confirm social customs, beliefs, and institutions by reference to tradition.

concepts.name: Binary opposition
concepts.definition: The concept that the human mind deals with pairs of contradictions or opposites, and myth functions to mediate between them.

concepts.name: Motifeme
concepts.definition: A unit of action or function in a myth, analogous to a morpheme or phoneme in linguistic analysis.

concepts.name: Quest
concepts.definition: A type of folktale or myth involving a search or journey, often with a specific goal.

concepts.name: Traditional tale
concepts.definition: A tale that belongs to a general class of stories, often with oral antecedents and structural patterns.

concepts.name: Structural theory
concepts.definition: An approach to myth interpretation focusing on the structure of tales, often involving motifemes and cultural/historical dimensions.

concepts.name: Comparative mythology
concepts.definition: The study of myths from different cultures to establish definitions and classifications.

concepts.name: Oral myth
concepts.definition: A myth that is transmitted orally, often considered pristine and timeless by some scholars.

concepts.name: Literary myth
concepts.definition: A myth that has been written down, often by a specific author, and may have oral antecedents.

concepts.name: Feminist interpretation
concepts.definition: An approach to mythology that focuses on the perspective of women and the psychological and social situation of female characters.

concepts.name: First wave feminism
concepts.definition: A stage in feminist analysis focusing on women's political, social, and economic liberation from and equality with men.

concepts.name: Second wave feminism
concepts.definition: A stage in feminist analysis emphasizing the inherent difference between men and women and the bond between women and nature.

concepts.name: Third wave feminism
concepts.definition: A deconstructive feminist approach focusing on difference, plurality, ambiguity, embodiment, the transitory, and the disruptive.

concepts.name: Rape
concepts.definition: Theme in mythology involving abduction or sexual violence, often with complex interpretations.

concepts.name: Chastity
concepts.definition: Force symbolized by devotion to Artemis, often associated with women.

concepts.name: Metamorphosis
concepts.definition: Transformation that saves the pursued from a fate worse than death.

concepts.name: Homosexuality
concepts.definition: Accepted and accommodated as part of life in the ancient world, with no prevailing hostile religious views condemning it as a sin.

concepts.name: Lesbianism
concepts.definition: Female homosexuality, derived from Sappho of Lesbos; less visible in mythology but present in subtexts.

concepts.name: Polis
concepts.definition: Greek city-state, fundamental in politics and mores, with marriage and family as core values.

concepts.name: Classical myth
concepts.definition: A story that, through its classical form, has attained a kind of immortality because its inherent archetypal beauty, profundity, and power have inspired rewarding renewal and transformation by successive generations.

concepts.name: catharsis
concepts.definition: An emotional and spiritual purging involving the emotions of pity and fear, possibly a goal for all serious mythic art.

concepts.name: mythos
concepts.definition: Plot; a well-constructed plot with a proper beginning, middle, and end, as defined by Aristotle in his Poetics.

concepts.name: historical myth
concepts.definition: A developed narrative that blends factual and mythical storytelling to provide insight into Greek interpretations of god and fate.

concepts.name: philosophical myth
concepts.definition: A distinct literary form developed by Plato, using myth for didactic purposes, such as the myth of Er about the soul and afterlife.

concepts.name: mythographer
concepts.definition: Late compilers of handbooks of mythology, such as Apollodorus, Pausanias, Hyginus, and Fulgentius.

concepts.name: Ur-myth
concepts.definition: The original version of a myth (oral or literary and usually hypothetical) sometimes designated as the Ur-myth.

concepts.name: thalassocracy
concepts.definition: Sea-power; Minoan Cnossus was a great thalassocracy.

concepts.name: labyrinth
concepts.definition: Maze-like structure; originally may have meant 'home of the double ax'.

concepts.name: labrys
concepts.definition: Double ax, a sacred symbol in Minoan religion.

concepts.name: Minoan
concepts.definition: Bronze Age civilization of Crete, named after King Minos.

concepts.name: Mycenaean
concepts.definition: Late Bronze Age civilization of mainland Greece, centered at Mycenae.

concepts.name: Cycladic
concepts.definition: Bronze Age culture of the Cyclades islands.

concepts.name: Helladic
concepts.definition: Bronze Age culture of mainland Greece (Hellas).

concepts.name: fertility mother-goddess
concepts.definition: A goddess associated with fertility, possibly worshiped in Neolithic and Minoan religion.

concepts.name: snake goddess
concepts.definition: A Minoan goddess depicted with snakes, associated with chthonic powers.

concepts.name: chthonic
concepts.definition: Relating to the earth or underworld.

concepts.name: Mycenaean civilization
concepts.definition: Civilization that reached its culmination in the Late Helladic period (1600-1100 B.C.); known for Cyclopean walls, tholos tombs, and Linear B script.

concepts.name: Minoan civilization
concepts.definition: Earlier civilization on Crete that influenced the Mycenaeans; worshiped a fertility mother-goddess.

concepts.name: Cyclopean walls
concepts.definition: Huge, monumental walls said to be built by the giant Cyclopes; typical of Mycenaean citadels.

concepts.name: tholos tombs
concepts.definition: Large beehive-shaped tombs built into hillsides; typical of Mycenaean civilization and confirming a belief in the afterlife.

concepts.name: megaron
concepts.definition: Central room with an open hearth in Mycenaean palaces.

concepts.name: Linear B
concepts.definition: Script used on clay tablets found in Mycenaean palaces; deciphered by Michael Ventris in 1952; contains names of Greek deities.

concepts.name: chthonian
concepts.definition: Relating to deities of the earth; concept merged with Olympian religion in Mycenaean times.

concepts.name: paean
concepts.definition: Title or epithet for Apollo; early form found in Linear B tablets.

concepts.name: potnia
concepts.definition: Word meaning 'mistress' or 'lady' in Linear B; suggests worship of a mother-fertility goddess.

concepts.name: solar eclipse
concepts.definition: An astronomical event where the moon blocks the sun, interpreted by Heraclitus and Plutarch in Homer's text.

concepts.name: Luwian
concepts.definition: An Indo-European language, a dialect of Hittite, used on a seal found at Troy.

concepts.name: Hittite
concepts.definition: Indo-European language of the Hittite Empire, used in diplomatic texts.

concepts.name: cuneiform
concepts.definition: A system of writing used for Hittite and other languages.

concepts.name: hieroglyphic Hittite
concepts.definition: A complex pictographic script used for Luwian.

concepts.name: Alaksandu treaty
concepts.definition: A Hittite text mentioning deities of Wilusa, including Appaliunas (Apollo).

concepts.name: Wilusa
concepts.definition: Hittite name for a city probably identified with Troy.

concepts.name: dactylic hexameter
concepts.definition: The meter of epic poetry, used in the Iliad and Odyssey, conducive to retention of historical fact and oral recitation.

concepts.name: Homeric questions
concepts.definition: Debates about the authorship, composition, and historicity of the Homeric epics.

concepts.name: oral poetry
concepts.definition: Poetry recited aloud, often with musical accompaniment, transmitted by bards like Phemius and Demodocus.

concepts.name: Homeridae
concepts.definition: A guild of professional rhapsodists who transmitted Homeric poetry.

concepts.name: Linear A
concepts.definition: Undeciphered script from Minoan Crete, not Greek.

concepts.name: Bronze Age
concepts.definition: Period of ancient Greek history, with chronology subject to scholarly debate.

concepts.name: Achaeans
concepts.definition: Term used in Homer, virtually equivalent to Mycenaean Greeks.

concepts.name: Chaos
concepts.definition: Primordial yawning void or unformed mass from which creation begins; in Hesiod, a gaping void; in Ovid, a crude unformed mass of elements.

concepts.name: Theogony
concepts.definition: A poem by Hesiod describing the genealogy and origins of the gods.

concepts.name: Works and Days
concepts.definition: A didactic poem by Hesiod about farming and justice, incorporating mythological stories.

concepts.name: Muses
concepts.definition: Goddesses of inspiration, daughters of Zeus, who reveal truth to poets.

concepts.name: Eros
concepts.definition: Primordial god of love and procreation, a potent force in creation myths.

concepts.name: World-egg
concepts.definition: A symbol in Orphic myth from which Eros (Phanes) hatches, representing the origin of creation.

concepts.name: Mystery religions
concepts.definition: Religious cults, such as Orphism, that involve secret rites and often focus on personal salvation.

concepts.name: Four elements
concepts.definition: Earth, air, fire, and water as primary materials of the universe, theorized by Empedocles.

concepts.name: Metamorphoses
concepts.definition: Ovid's poem focusing on stories of transformation, providing a late Roman mythological survey.

concepts.name: hieros gamos
concepts.definition: Sacred marriage, a recurring archetype in mythology where sky-god and earth-goddess unite to ensure fertility.

concepts.name: matriarchy
concepts.definition: Social system where the female is primary; reflected in the primacy of Gaia in Hesiod's Theogony.

concepts.name: patriarchy
concepts.definition: Social system where the male is supreme; reflected in later myths where sky-god becomes dominant.

concepts.name: Cyclopes
concepts.definition: One-eyed giants, children of Uranus and Gaia, who forged Zeus's thunderbolt.

concepts.name: Hecatonchires
concepts.definition: Hundred-handed, fifty-headed giants, children of Uranus and Gaia.

concepts.name: Oceanids
concepts.definition: Daughters and sons of Oceanus and Tethys, spirits of rivers, waters, and springs.

concepts.name: Titans
concepts.definition: Twelve children of Uranus and Gaia, deifications of natural aspects, important for their progeny.

concepts.name: Styx
concepts.definition: Dread river of the Underworld, used for solemn oaths by the gods.

concepts.name: Ambrosia
concepts.definition: Food of the gods, given to Tithonus by Eos.

concepts.name: Nectar
concepts.definition: Divine drink, shed by Helius on Leucothoë's corpse to create the frankincense tree.

concepts.name: castration complex
concepts.definition: Freudian concept of male unconscious fear of being deprived of sexual potency, stemming from guilt over hatred of father and desire for mother.

concepts.name: Golden Age
concepts.definition: Mythical period of peace and prosperity under Cronus' rule.

concepts.name: sacred marriage
concepts.definition: Union of sky and earth deities, reenacted by Cronus and Rhea.

concepts.name: etiological myth
concepts.definition: Myth that explains the origin of a practice, natural phenomenon, or institution.

concepts.name: Titanomachy
concepts.definition: The ten-year war between Zeus and the Olympians against Cronus and the Titans.

concepts.name: Gigantomachy
concepts.definition: The battle between the Olympian gods and the giants (Gegeneis) born from Earth.

concepts.name: Gegeneis
concepts.definition: Earthborn giants produced by Ge to challenge the gods.

concepts.name: Silver Age
concepts.definition: Second age; humans were foolish and impious, destroyed by Zeus.

concepts.name: Age of Heroes
concepts.definition: Fourth age; demigods who fought at Thebes and Troy; some dwell in the Islands of the Blessed.

concepts.name: Iron Age
concepts.definition: Fifth and current age; characterized by toil, wickedness, and eventual destruction by Zeus.

concepts.name: Hellenistic sculpture
concepts.definition: Sculptural style characterized by melodramatic, emotional intensity, contrasting with classical restraint.

concepts.name: Pandora's box
concepts.definition: A later misinterpretation of Pandora's jar (pithos) as a box (pyxis), popularized by Erasmus in 1508.

concepts.name: Hope
concepts.definition: The only thing remaining in Pandora's jar after evils escape; its nature is ambiguous—either a blessing or a curse.

concepts.name: Blind hopes
concepts.definition: Hopes given by Prometheus to mortals to prevent them from foreseeing their fate, as described in Aeschylus' Prometheus Bound.

concepts.name: Succession Myth
concepts.definition: Archetypal motif of a younger god overthrowing an older one to gain power, seen in Greek and Near Eastern myths.

concepts.name: Flood archetype
concepts.definition: Universal myth motif of a great flood sent by gods to punish humanity, with a few survivors repopulating the earth.

concepts.name: Divine Child
concepts.definition: Motif of a god or hero who grows up in nature and overcomes challenges to achieve power.

concepts.name: Dragonslayer
concepts.definition: Archetypal hero or god who slays a dragon, symbolizing triumph over chaos.

concepts.name: Enuma Elish
concepts.definition: Babylonian Epic of Creation, named after its opening words 'When on high...'.

concepts.name: Ziggurat
concepts.definition: Temple tower characteristic of Mesopotamian religious architecture.

concepts.name: aegis
concepts.definition: A shield with miraculous protective powers, originally a shepherd's cloak, associated with Zeus.

concepts.name: Olympic Games
concepts.definition: Principal athletic festival in the ancient world, reorganized in 776 BCE, said to have been founded by Heracles.

concepts.name: Eleusinian Mysteries
concepts.definition: Dominant matriarchal mysteries associated with Demeter, refusing to submit to patriarchy.

concepts.name: Oracle
concepts.definition: A place or priestess through which a god gives prophetic responses, often through omens or inspired speech.

concepts.name: Chthonic hero
concepts.definition: A hero associated with the underworld and fertility, often consulted in subterranean settings.

concepts.name: erastes
concepts.definition: In Athenian pederastic relationships, the older active lover.

concepts.name: eromenos
concepts.definition: In Athenian pederastic relationships, the younger passive beloved.

concepts.name: thiasos
concepts.definition: An entourage of satyrs and maenads accompanying Dionysus.

concepts.name: Homeric Hymn to Ares
concepts.definition: A relatively late composition invoking Ares with astrological reference to the planet Mars, portraying him as a complex god providing courage.

concepts.name: Moira
concepts.definition: Abstract concept of fate, often singular, closely linked to Luck (Tyche) and Necessity (Ananke). The relation of gods to destiny is variously depicted; sometimes Zeus is supreme, other times even Zeus must bow to Fate.

concepts.name: Moirai
concepts.definition: The three Fates (Clotho, Lachesis, Atropos) who spin, measure, and cut the thread of life, determining destiny.

concepts.name: Olympiads
concepts.definition: System of dating by the Olympic Games, celebrated every four years after 776 BC.

concepts.name: Panhellenic festival
concepts.definition: A festival to which all Hellenes came, such as the Olympic Games and the Pythian Games at Delphi.

concepts.name: Anthropomorphism
concepts.definition: Conception of deities as human in form and character.

concepts.name: Ichor
concepts.definition: Substance clearer than blood flowing in gods' veins.

concepts.name: Demigod
concepts.definition: Offspring of a god and a mortal, with limited powers and mortal.

concepts.name: Hero
concepts.definition: Mortal honored with cult after death, associated with chthonic powers.

concepts.name: Polytheism
concepts.definition: Belief in many gods, expansive and able to incorporate new divinities.

concepts.name: Monotheism
concepts.definition: Belief in one supreme god, emerging within Greek polytheism.

concepts.name: Humanism
concepts.definition: Greek variety emphasizing human potential and achievement.

concepts.name: Fate
concepts.definition: Force to which even Zeus may be subject.

concepts.name: hubris
concepts.definition: Dangerous pride or arrogance that leads to downfall; a theme in Greek tragedy.

concepts.name: Nemesis
concepts.definition: Divine retribution or vengeance against hubris.

concepts.name: jealous god
concepts.definition: Concept of a deity who is envious of human happiness and causes trouble.

concepts.name: Purification
concepts.definition: Ritual cleansing of a murderer, performed by Croesus for Adrastus.

concepts.name: Ate
concepts.definition: Goddess of doom and destruction, associated with Atys.

concepts.name: Adrasteia
concepts.definition: Another name for Nemesis, meaning 'necessity'.

concepts.name: dithyramb
concepts.definition: Sacred choral song performed in honor of Dionysus.

concepts.name: hecatomb
concepts.definition: Sacrifice of a hundred cattle.

concepts.name: Panathenaea
concepts.definition: Annual festival honoring Athena Polias, depicted on the Parthenon frieze.

concepts.name: heorte
concepts.definition: General Greek term for 'festival', derived from word for 'banquet'.

concepts.name: Hecatombaion
concepts.definition: First month of the Attic year, during which Hecatombaia and Panathenaea were held.

concepts.name: Anthesterion
concepts.definition: Month during which Anthesteria festival was celebrated.

concepts.name: Anthesteria
concepts.definition: Spring festival in honor of Dionysus, celebrating new wine, with elements of death and rebirth.

concepts.name: Brauronia
concepts.definition: Festival in honor of Artemis.

concepts.name: Thesmophoria
concepts.definition: Women's festival in honor of Demeter.

concepts.name: Great Dionysia
concepts.definition: Festival established in 6th century B.C. in Athens, where tragedies and comedies were performed in honor of Dionysus.

concepts.name: chthonic cult
concepts.definition: Cult honoring heroes or chthonic powers, with rituals differing from Olympian worship (e.g., blood poured on ground).

concepts.name: Seer
concepts.definition: A professional diviner who interprets signs from the gods, such as bird flight, dreams, and entrails.

concepts.name: Augury
concepts.definition: Interpretation of omens, especially from birds, as part of divination.

concepts.name: Extispicy
concepts.definition: Examination of animal entrails for divination.

concepts.name: Hepatoscopy
concepts.definition: Examination of the liver specifically for divination.

concepts.name: Sacrifice
concepts.definition: The most significant religious act in Greek ritual, involving the offering of an animal to a deity.

concepts.name: Temenos
concepts.definition: A sacred precinct cut off from the profane world, where sacrifices are performed.

concepts.name: Ololuge
concepts.definition: The ritual cry uttered by women at the climax of a sacrifice, expressing joy or emotional release.

concepts.name: Splanchna
concepts.definition: The internal organs of a sacrificial animal, roasted and eaten by important participants.

concepts.name: Theophrastus
concepts.definition: Greek philosopher and successor of Aristotle who attributed three functions to sacrifice: to honor the god, to give thanks, and to persuade the god to grant a blessing.

concepts.name: Walter Burkert
concepts.definition: Anthropologist who argued that sacrificial ritual elements trace back to preagricultural hunting practices and aimed to allay fear and anxiety at killing an animal.

concepts.name: Jean-Pierre Vernant
concepts.definition: Scholar who interpreted sacrificial ritual as a festive celebration establishing social and religious hierarchy and cohesion.

concepts.name: Earthshaker
